subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE ON WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.

speechtext:
Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, to authorize the board to provide pensions for members, officers and employees and to make provision for the increase of the fixed minimum price on wheat deliveries; to extend the control of international movements of wheat products and to empower the governor in council to extend the present system to oats or barley.
He said: The purposes and essential features of the bill to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, which will be founded on this resolution, are fourfold, as follows: (a) to make provision for pensions for members, officers and employees of the board; (b) to provide authority to increase the SI.35 fixed minimum price, and to make corresponding increases in payments to producers who have delivered, or will deliver, wheat to the board within the five-year pool period; (c) to extend the control of interprovincial movements of wheat to wheat products; (d) to empower the governor in council, by regulation, to extend to oats or barley the regulations now applicable to wheat.
The proposed amendments are important to every grower of wheat and coarse grains, and in fact to consumers of coarse grains. Growers of wheat will find an urgency in the passage of these amendments. The first' three amendments should not be contentious, and while there may be differences of opinion regarding the wisdom of the fourth amendment, I trust that debate at least in the resolution stage need not be unduly prolonged.
Before discussing the merits of the amendments, it may be worthwhile to review briefly the history of the wheat board and its present responsibilities. The origin of the Canadian wheat board can be traced back to the board of grain supervisors established in 1917, which directed the marketing of Canada's wheat during the war period and until 1920 when it was abolished. The government resumed its activity in wheat marketing in 1931 by undertaking stabilization activities which unfortunately failed in their objective in that there was little stability in wheat prices from 1931 to 1935.
The present Canadian wheat board was established under the Canadian Wheat Board Act of July 5, 1935. The board now consists of three commissioners and an eleven-man * advisory committee. The primary function of the board has remained the handling of wheat, but during the war in particular it was assigned a number of other functions, such as rationing elevator space, handling, on various occasions, flaxseed, soy beans, sunflower seed, rapeseed, the equalization funds for oats and barley, the administration of drawbacks in respect to flour and other wheat products, and the minimum support and ceiling prices for
Canadian Wheat Board Act

oats and barley. The most important change in general policy took place in 1943, when the government took over, through the board, all stocks of unsold cash wheat and stopped trading in wheat futures on the Winnipeg grain exchange. At that time the board became the monopoly trader in all wheat moving in interprovincial or international channels.
Throughout the war years, Canada provided practically all the import wheat consumed in the United Kingdom, and special arrangements were made to give the United Kingdom priority in obtaining its continuing requirements of wheat. In 1946 a four-year contract was made between Canada and the United Kingdom, involving purchase by the United Kingdom of 600 million bushels of wheat in the four year period ending July 31. 1950. In order to enable Canada to carry out its obligations under this contract, the wheat crops grown m the years 1945, 1916, 1947, 1948 and 1949 were pooled, and the present wheat pool act provides that initial payments on wheat delivered to the pool will be based on S 1.35 per bushel.
The la9t ten years have seen a full cycle of problems in the marketing of Canadian wheat. The first phase from 1938 to 1942 saw the steady accumulation of record supplies, which reached a carryover of some 600 million bushels in July 1943. During this period, the handling and storing of these unprecedented quantities of wheat was the major administrative concern of the board. In the second phase, from 1942 to date, somewhat lower production and increasing demand has reversed the trend and the problem is becoming one of moving stocks to seaboard as rapidly as possible. The carryover was reduced to 73 million bushels, as at July 31, 1946, and will probably be little more than that at the end of the current crop year.
As would be expected, in the light of these huge shifts in the supply and demand situation, major adjustments have been required from time to time in board policies, and amendments to the wheat act have in fact been necessary each year. This year is not an exception. Although there is no important new element in the picture, the continued failure of supply to overtake demand has created new situations, which render further amendments to the wheat board act desirable.
An obvious requirement is a pension fund for the staff of the board. The Canadian wheat board has been operating continuously since 1935, and up to the present time, but no provision has been made for a pension for any member of the staff. The proposed amendment provides the board with authority to establish a pension fund with the approval of the

governor in council. A scheme is contemplated which would require contributions equally from employees and the board. The contributions of the board to the fund would be considered part of the expenses of the board's operations. This is, of course, increasingly recognized today as a necessary expense of doing business. It may be questioned whether, on balance, it should be considered merely as an expense. In many cases, the automatic saving and security provided by a pension are valued more than an equivalent increase in pay, enabling the employer to hold trained personnel and to reduce costly turnover. When the bill is in committee I shall be able to give figures as to the number of employees involved and the approximate cost, but I think it is sufficient to say, at this stage, that it is intended that the pension plan, when introduced, will be similar to the superannuation provisions for civil servants generally.
The second amendment deals with an increase in the initial payment for wheat delivered to the five-year pool. Practically final results on two of the five years involved in the pool are now available. The 1945 wheat deliveries totalled 235-4 million bushels, and the Canadian wheat board holds a surplus of approximately $44,000,000 on this crop. The 1946 deliveries totalled 333 million bushels and the board holds a surplus of about $110 million derived from this crop.
The 1947-48 crop year is more than half completed, so it is possible to make fairly close calculations for this current year. The board estimates wheat deliveries at only 270 millions, which leaves about 20 million bushels for sale at class 2 price, outside the domestic and United Kingdom markets. Most of the wheat is either sold, or is committed, at the fixed domestic or United Kingdom prices. Therefore, it is fairly safe to estimate that there will be a surplus of about $80,000,000 on the 1947 crop.
There are, of course, many unknown factors concerning the 1948 and 1949 crops at this time. We do not know what the production and marketing will be, and our assumptions can only proceed on the basis of average crops. The market possibilities are also somewhat obscure but the Canada-United Kingdom wheat agreement provides for the sale of 140 millions at $2.00 per bushel in 1948-49 and the same quantity in 1949-50, the price for this latter year to be settled later. We must re-emphasize that there are major hazards in attempting, at this time, to arrive at the financial position of the five-year pool as at its terminal date, July 31, 1950, when

__________ Canadian Wheat Board Act
we now have complete information for two crops, incomplete information for the current year, and only a few guides for the last two crop years.
However, it does now appear that the guaranteed initial payment of $1.35 a bushel for No. 1 Manitoba northern, basis Fort William-Port Arthur or Vancouver, provided for in the act, is lower than necessary to maintain a prudent margin over the five-year period. It is consequently proposed to raise that payment. The proposed increase will, of course, be applicable to the 1945, 1946 and 1947 crops already delivered or being delivered, and to the 1948 and 1949 crops.
The amount of the new initial payment, or sum certain, is not included in the bill. Instead, the government is taking power to increase the initial payment from time to time, whenever the cash position of the pool would appear to justify such action. Any such increases in initial payment will of course be retroactive to producers who have already sold and delivered wheat to the pool, within the pool period, and will represent a guaranteed price for future deliveries of wheat to the pool, for the balance of the pool period. It is the wish of the government that, if prices continue strong, the advantage shall not be withheld from the producer, and that steps shall be taken to pass on the benefits as quickly as the circumstances may warrant.
The amount of the increase in the initial payment now contemplated will not be announced until this bill becomes law. The reason, I think, is obvious. Should these amendments fail to receive approval, the government would have no power to increase the amount of the initial payment that is at present specified in the wheat board act. There would be no purpose in debating the subject of price at this time, as this must be a matter for the government to decide. I am sure that there will be less confusion and less expenditure of time if we consider the amendments covered by the resolution which have to do with the general principles of procedure and operation of the board, without bringing in the question of the amount of the proposed increase in the initial payment.
The third amendment proposes to include control of wheat products as well as wheat. The Canadian Wheat Board Act now prohibits the sale or movement of wheat from one province to another province, or outside Canada, unless the wheat is the property of the board or the movement is permitted by it. There is, however, no control over the movement of wheat products across provincial boundaries. I am advised by the wheat board *849-107
that, since something over 100 million bushels of w'heat are now annually milled in Canada, of which about half is for the domestic market, the lack of control over interprovincial movements of flour could be a source of serious weakness in maintaining effective control of the basic wheat situation.
The fourth amendment proposes to empower the governor in council by regulation to extend to oats and barley the regulations now applicable to wheat. Strong representations favouring the marketing of oats and barley through the wheat board have been received from farm organizations in both western and eastern Canada, among them the Canadian council of agriculture. The government desires to meet the wishes of farm organizations in this regard, provided a workable plan can be agreed upon. However, the government is well aware that the compulsory marketing of oats and barley through the board represents serious difficulties. The success of such an enterprise must be dependent on a large measure of agreement on policy matters as between organized farmers of both the producer and the consumer class, as well as on the co-operation of provincial governments. Therefore this government will wish to have concrete evidence of such agreement and such co-operation before it can assume the responsibility for putting this amendment into effect.
The difficulties of which I speak stem from the basically different uses made of wheat on the one hand and of oats and barley on the other. Wheat is pre-eminently a grain for human consumption, "the staff of life," the most efficient and economical foodstuff known to the human race. About three bushels out of every four of the Canadian crop are consumed as food by people at home and abroad and, of the balance, about half is required for seeding the next crop. The great bulk of the crop-on the average over eighty per cent- must be moved across interprovincial and international boundaries. Consequently the federal government can, under its legal responsibilities, regulate and have effective control of the wheat trade as a whole.
Oats and barley, on the other hand, are preeminently animal feed crops. Human use, including porridge, beer and whisky, amounts to less than two per cent of the oats crop and five per cent of the barley crop of Canada. In fact, only about thirty per cent of the oats and forty per cent of the barley ever leave the farms on which they are grown, except in the form of livestock. A large proportion of these grains that leave the farm are sold as feed or seed to other farmers. In recent years only about twenty per cent of the prairie oat and
Canadian Wheat Board Act

barley crops have moved, under the government's freight assistance policy, to eastern Canada or to British Columbia. Incidentally this is a far greater proportion of the crop than had ever moved out of the prairie provinces prior to the initiation of the government's freight assistance policy.
Normally a relatively insignificant portion of these crops moves into export. In short, the movement of oats and barley is from farmer to farmer. This presents peculiar problems in establishing and maintaining prices which would be accepted as fair in both the east and west, under a federal government monopoly of interprovincial trade. To put it another way: while the wheat board is handling wheat it is primarily concerned-to quote the Canadian Wheat Board Act-with "promoting the sale of grain, produced in Canada, in world markets." The wheat board, in handling oats and barley, would be concerned primarily with sales of western grain to eastern farmers, at prices that both seller and buyer will consider fair and reasonable. I am informed that at a recent meeting of the Canadian federation of agriculture this possible conflict of interest between farmer buyers and farmer sellers was recognized.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE ON WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Was that "recognized" or "reconciled"?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE ON WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Recognized. The point I am making is that while wheat, oats and barley are all classed as grains, their marketing, from the point of view of their place in the whole mechanism of production and trade, as well as their use and customary manner of handling, are quite different and distinct. This raises not only practical marketing problems but also constitutional questions. As my colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) observed last year, speaking of the dominion government entering this field alone-if I may be allowed to paraphrase him-a scheme that would work for oats and barley would not be constitutional, and a constitutional scheme would not work.
It is with this dilemma in mind that we are introducing the present legislation. There is no question of the dominion's constitutional authority to regulate interprovincial trade or export trade in oats and barley, but there is very considerable doubt as to whether that limited power would in itself provide effective control of commodities which are so largely marketed locally. This amendment to the wheat board act will open the door as far as the federal government is concerned. The next step will be to determine whether the three provincial governments most directly con-

cerned-that is, in the prairie provinces-wish to join with us in placing compulsory regulation of the trade in oats and barley in the hands of the wheat board.
Presumably this could be done most conveniently by use of the device known as "conjoint" or "complementary" legislation. The device of "enabling" legislation, once employed in a number of fields of agricultural production marketing, has been held ultra vires by the privy council as a method of delegating provincial powers to the dominion. Co-operative arrangements have, however, been worked out and given the force of law in several fields of agricultural marketing, by "conjoint" or "complementary" legislation. In such cases the province or provinces concerned that wish to take advantage of the dominion legislation pass directly whatever complementary legislation is necessary and within their power, and appoint the dominion administrative agents as provincial agents as well. This may perhaps indicate a path for provincial co-operation which must be a preliminary to bringing this legislation into force.
The government is prepared to take whatever steps lie within its power to assist in establishing marketing arrangements that will help to maintain economic and stable prices for Canadian agricultural products. The government must, however, be satisfied that any given scheme for this purpose is a practical one, a constitutional one, a workable one and one that will command the support of the interested groups concerned. Until it is satisfied that these conditions have been met, the government will not be prepared to undertake the marketing of oats and barley through the wheat board. It will be noted in the resolution that marketing arrangements shall come into force only at the beginning of a crop year. I believe the attitude of the government in this regard will be understood by all hon. members who are familiar with grain marketing and related agricultural problems.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE ON WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very attentively and1 certainly with interest to the address just delivered by the new Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) on this resolution which reads:
Resolved, that it is expedient to present a bill to am and the Canadian Wheat Board Act, to authorize the board to provide pensions for members, officers and employees and to make provision for the increase of the fixed minimum price on wheat deliveries; to extend the control of interprovincial movements of wheat products and to empower the governor in council to extend the present system to oats or barley.
The minister commenced his remarks by stating he thought the first two or three items

Canadian Wheat Board Act
would not be controversial but that certainly the third might cause considerable debate. As he expounded his views on the resolution I think he certainly proved to this house that several of the amendments now being proposed will be rather contentious.
The minister said the wheat board act came into being in 1935 and that the first important change was made in 1943, when it took over the handling of all wheat in this country, I believe under the war measures act. Then he went on to deal with the various amendments proposed. The first had to do with pensions. He pointed out that authority was to be given to the board to provide pensions for its officers and employees on a contributory basis, fifty per cent being contributed by the employees and fifty per cent by the board, which means that, since the board's contribution comes out of the board's funds, ultimately that portion of the cost will be borne by the grain producers of the country.
Then the minister went on to deal with the initial payment, and made the remarkable statement that the amount of the initial payment would not be embodied in the bill. He set forth the surplus for the 1945 crop year, which we all realize is the last complete year we have, since the complete report for 1946 is not in yet. The minister gave an estimate of $110 million and' a further estimate for the crop year 1947, which we are about half way through, of some $80,000,000. I believe the total of the figures he gave is about $234 million. The amount he gave for 1945 is not identical with the surplus shown in the wheat board report for that year but the two figures are within a few million of each other; and in these days, with all the things the minister is doing and all the things he did in the past, I suppose we should1 not quibble about a few million dollars.
I do not know whether it is parliamentary to term a bill political trickery, but honestly I have never seen another bill of this nature introduced in this house. The minister went on to speak of the third amendment, which will deal with the movement of wheat products within the country; and the fourth, which he said from the start might be very controversial. The minister said compulsory marketing often gives rise to very serious difficulties, and I believe he referred to a statement made some time ago by the law officers of the crown. This all seems remarkable when we think of the debate that took place in this house about a year ago on another bill to amend the wheat board act. That bill was passed by this house on March 13, 1947, and during the discussion there was quite a controversy. At that time no mration whatever 5849-1074
was made of the amount of wheat to be delivered to the United Kingdom during the four-year period referred to; and that point has been mentioned again today. Nor during those discussions was there any mention in the bill of the price to be paid by the United Kingdom under that contract. So when anyone says that after many objections and amendments to the bill of last year a great many on this side of the house voted for the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement in its entirety. I maintain that is hardly the fact. I voted for the Canadian wheat board, as I have always done, and I continue to be a supporter of the board. But I want to say we have never had an opportunity in this house to vote on the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement by itself, in its entirety.

speechtext:
I followed the debate closely; I have read Hansard carefully several times, and I maintain that is not a fact. We have never opposed the gift to Britain. We have always said they deserved it, and that by all means we should give it to them, but that the cost should be borne by the taxpayers of Canada. We have never voted to saddle the producers of this country with that unfair burden, nor were we ever given the opportunity to vote on that question by itself. In the debate last year the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) moved an amendment, which is to be found at page 857 of Hansard for February 27, 1947, as follows:
The provisions of this act shall be made applicable to oats, barley, rye and flax, and shall mutatis mutandis apply to such kind of grain as they apply to wheat.
I followed the hon. member, and at page 858 of Hansard I opposed such legislation as giving altogether too much power to the government to proceed by order in council. I have always opposed legislation by order in council in peacetime. I went on to say:
Today our producers have no idea how their coarse grains may be handled during this coming crop year-
That was in 1947, and the same thing is going to apply in 1948. I could go into a great deal of detail, but I can tell you there is quite a controversy among the barley producers of the west as to what their plans should be for 1948, especially if the embargo is continued which shuts them out from their natural market for malting barley. Following my remarks last year the Minister of Agriculture had this to say, also at page 858:
I 'am quite certain that neither the farm organization nor the farmers generally would want the act to go quite that far . . . Wheat,
Canadian Wheat Board Act

as we grow it in -western Canada, is grown intentionally for -the purpose of feeding human beings . . . Therefore we set down a certain method of marketing it. Oats and barley, on the other hand . . . are grains which are grown largely for the purpose of feeding them on the farms where they are grown or of selling them from one farmer to another-
I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce covered that same point in his remarks a few moments ago. Following that the Minister of Justice had this to say, at pages 865 and 866:
. . . wheat being mainly an export commodity . . . we think we keep within the confines of our constitutional powers when we deal with wheat. I said I had never seen such a bill introduced in this house, nor had I read of such a bill in the history of this nation. I think those of us who have lived with this wheat board act will agree that the board was brought into being to market wheat, which is an export commodity, and to obtain the best price possible for the producers. I do not think there is any argument at all about that. Throughout the war years, under -the war measures act, and today by legislation the board has been and is being used as a price control agency, to keep the price down. Instead of setting floor prices for the -producers it is setting ceiling prices. It has been subsidizing the consumers of Canada and Great Britain and is doing so today. That was not the original thought when the wheat board was brought into being. I have pointed out at various times in the past what the operations of this board and price control measures in Canada have cost *the producers of this country. I know there is some argument about having exact figures in the matter. However I have used the Searle index in the past, and I shall continue to use it. Speaking in the house at this session I pointed out that according to their figures, from 1943 until December 1947 wheat producers had suffered a loss of $857 million, represented by the difference between the

world price and the price offered by the Canadian wheat board. I repeat that statement. That is what it cost Canadian producers in the matter of wheat alone.
The minster has dealt with figures to which I have already referred relating to surpluses for three years, both actual and estimated. I placed a question on the order paper, in response to which I received a return, and in that return are figures showing the bushels of wheat handled by the wheat board in 1945. The bushelage is placed at 237,297.000, and the surplus in the report is $39,000,000 some odd. The total bushels of wheat handled by the board in 1946 is given as 335,108,000, and for 1947, the present marketing year, it is estimated that the board will handle 270,278,000 bushels.	The total for three years is
842,684,414 bushels of wheat. That is what I presume we are chiefly concerned about in the resolution at -this time, namely the total bushels of wheat handled by the board in those three years.
The total figures the minister put on record a few minutes ago amounted to $234,000,000, actual and estimated. So that is the amount which will have to be divided over this amount of wheat. I cannot for the life of me understand why an initial payment price is not embodied in the bill at this time. Once we were away from the house last year the exminister of trade and commerce made speeches throughout the country, and other ministers of the government also made speeches, stating that there would be payment of at least 20 cents a bushel made as soon as parliament assembled at this present session. Now we have before us this vague measure suggesting that in the amending legislation no price will be embodied in the bill. We have that factor. There has been reference to the movement of wheat products, and the suggestion has been made by order in council as to how oats or barley may be handled. The minister himself points out in the same remarks just how unconstitutional the matter is.
If there ever was a measure brought into parliament for members of the government to flout at election time across this country, to play it both ways, then you certainly have it in this measure.

I hope he spoke in the same terms to them that he used to the labour men who approached him at the golf club.
I have listened attentively to the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) dealing with this matter from his point of view, and I have also read the motion on the order paper. After reading the motion on the order paper I shall have to agree that the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) has analysed it very well. It is distinctly a political document. I do not know that the minister who is piloting it through the house is responsible for it, but it has all the earmarks of our fellow Saskatchewan citizen the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). It certainly is worded in such a way that there is no earthly excuse for it, Mr. Speaker.
The amendment of the Progressive Conservative party asked that it be split into three bills. There is absolutely no reason why that should not be done. The motion that we are asked to deal with now is either a railroad motion or a delaying action motion, one or the other. It can only have one of two purposes to serve, so far as I can see. If we want these payments made immediately, and we do, then we must accept everything in the motion, regardless. If we want this matter of coarse grains to be included in the operation of the wheat board carefully considered by a committee of the whole house, or by a special committee, or by a standing committee, then we must be prepared to delay the payment for wheat on the 1945, 1946 and 1947 crops. There is no sound reason for the motion having been put before the house in that way. It could just as well have come before us in three bills as moved in the amendment by the hon. member for Souris. We certainly have three things to consider in it: one is the matter of pensions to the employees of the wheat board. I do not think anybody in this house will oppose that particular thing. A motion to do that would have passed without very much consideration. Probably a few questions with regard to amounts and conditions of payment would have been asked. Certainly no violent controversy would have been generated because of a bill of that kind. Very few hon. members, if any, even though they may not wish to see a further payment made on the wheat delivered to the board since 1945, even though they may not wish it in their hearts, would have had the courage to rise in their places and say so. Therefore I am safe in saying that there would have been no opposition to a motion to bring in a bill to authorize the government, the wheat board or the appropriate body, to make that payment.
On the third question there will certainly be controversy. There will be large numbers in the Progressive Conservative ranks who will disagree with even the slight implication in the motion on the order paper to include oats or barley in the operations of the wheat board. Since 1935 we have known that the principle embodied in this motion will find many opponents among the Liberal ranks, because going back to 1935 when the bill was originally introduced in the house we find that the official opposition, which was then the Liberal party, was successful in having, through its
Canadian Wheat Board Act

debate in opposition, the compulsory features of this bill deleted, namely, sections 9, 10, 11, and 16, which provided the penalties if those compulsory features were disobeyed. Therefore we can expect to find a great deal of opposition there. The government is not concerned whether oats or barley or both are included in the operation of the wheat board. They would prefer that they were not included, but they put the resolution on the order paper in such a way as to indicate to the fellow farmers of the Minister of Agriculture in Saskatchewan that he and his godson are down here fighting the battle of the farmers of the west.

If hon. gentlemen will wait until their turn comes they can have all the time they wish and I shall listen politely to them. I do not want to weary the house too much, but I will go back to 1932, which is quite a little while ago. I hold in my hand the eighth annual report of the Saskatchewan Co-operative Wheat Producers Limited, as they were at that time, commonly called the wheat pool, and I shall refer to them as the wheat pool from now on because the wheat has been taken out of the name and they are now the Saskatchewan Co-operative Producers Limited, but they are the organization from which these reports come. On page 20 of the eighth annual report they say:
Your board is of the opinion that, until some measure of economic stability has been attained, it will be in the best interests of western Canada if a national marketing organization is set up with complete authority to market the Canadian crop. In order to achieve this end it is probable that legislation will be required both from the provincial and federal parliaments.
That was in 1932, giving an account of the operations of the crop year 1931-32. The following year, 1933, the same organization, reporting on the year just under review, had this to say on page 29:
Following out the decision of the delegates at the last annual meeting, to submit a request for a national marketing agency with complete control over the marketing of the entire crop, every effort was made, in co-operation with the provincial wheat pools of Manitoba and Alberta, to secure action by the federal government.
I want those people who claim to have assisted in the organization of the wheat pool in the early days to remember these statements, because they are going to continue in similar vein right to the end. I take the tenth annual report, 1934, dealing with the period under review, and on page 44 they say:
Your board is more than ever convinced that international co-operation holds the key to better times, and we believe that the establishment of a national marketing agency, with complete control over the Canadian crop, will place Canada in a first-class position to work with the 5849-108
other nations of the world, both exporters and importers, in an effort to find a solution to the present impasse.

Mr. Speaker, like the two hon. members who have preceded me, I also regret that the government has seen fit to bring down a resolution embodying four separate proposals: to provide pensions for members, officers and employees; to make provision for the increase of the fixed minimum price on wheat deliveries; to extend the control of interprovincial movements of wheat products, and to empower the governor in council to extend the present system to oats or barley. Obviously including four proposals in the resolution is bound to delay passage of the bill. Today the farmers are anxiously awaiting an announcement of government policy regarding the increase in the amount of the initial payment. I say they are anxiously awaiting the announcement, but they are even more anxiously awaiting payment. That is especially true in the drought areas, where many farmers have not had a good crop for over two years. They are in sore need of this money to finance their spring operations. I am afraid bringing the resolution down in this form is going to delay passage of the bill and thereby delay the making of these payments. Just on that point I would suggest to the minister that when the payments finally are made the policy of last year be followed again this year and the payments made first in the drought areas, where the farmers are in so much greater need of money than in other parts of the country.
For these reasons we are prepared to support the amendment of the Progressive Conservative party. As a matter of fact, we hope the government will be prepared to accept that amendment and bring down three separate bills, the first being the bill relating to the increase in the initial payment. Generally speaking I may say we favour the four proposals contained in the resolution. The criticism we have to offer will be with regard to the degree of the proposals rather than the proposals themselves. We support the continuation of the wheat board as the sole marketing agency for wheat. Furthermore we believe it is to the advantage of the farmer
Canadian Wheat Board Act

to have a long term stabilization program rather than to capitalize on short time high level prices; and I am satisfied that the overwhelming majority of the farmers of Canada are in favour of such a policy. I suggest to the minister that the reason there is such widespread criticism of the government's wheat policy today is that it is neither one thing nor the other. On the one hand it denies the farmer the present high prices; on the other hand it fails to guarantee prices in the future beyond 1949. It has forced the Canadian farmer to subsidize the British consumer and has allowed the prices of goods the farmer has to buy to rise substantially while at the same time placing ceilings on Canadian farm produce. So is it any wonder the farmers of the west are discontented with the government's wheat policy?
Let me review briefly some of the main causes for this discontent. In the first place the government's wheat policy is supposed to be a policy of stabilization. Thus far, however, that policy has failed to materialize. On September 19, 1945, the then minister of trade and commerce, announcing the government's post-war wheat policy, had this to say as reported at page 289 of Hansard for 1945:
It is in the interest of Canada and of Canadian wheat growers that the importing countries should continue to obtain Canadian wheat at prices not in excess of those prevailing at the *end of hostilities. Accordingly the government, By order in council, has instructed the Canadian wheat board to offer wheat for sale for export overseas at prices not higher than the current export price of $1.55 per bushel, basis No. 1 northern, in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver.
In asking Canadian producers to forgo such benefits as might be realized in the short run through higher export prices, the government recognizes the paramount need for relative stability of income to wheat producers. Toward this end, the government undertakes, that in the five-year period ending July 31, 1950, producers will receive not less than $1 per bushel, basis No. 1 northern, in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver on the authorized deliveries for each crop year. For the balance of the 1945-46 crop year at least, the Canadian wheat board initial advance will continue at $1.25, where it was set two years ago.
And farther on:
Any further increase in wheat prices now would aggravate the problems of economic and political readjustment of the liberated areas to Canada's detriment in future trade with those areas. There is a moral obligation not to take advantage of our recent allies in their time of compelling need.
I should like to quote the reply I made at that time to this new policy. Speaking on behalf of this group, and as reported at page 469 of Hansard, I said:
We insist that when Canada makes that sacrifice and that contribution it should be a

sacrifice of the Canadian people and not of any one class of society alone. Why should .agriculture be asked to stand the full cost of that sacrifice? Surely -the logical thing to do is to pay the farmers the price that can be obtained, sell the commodity to the people who need it, at the current price, and make up the difference betwreen the two figures out of the general revenue fund or any other source which the government sees fit to use. We may differ as to the way that should be done, but that is not the point in question now.
The minister has tried to excuse his proposals on the ground that the government policy will compensate the farmers by guaranteeing a floor price of $1 a bushel for the next five years. But the mere fact that the minister says that it will be compensating them implies that the price may fall below that figure. On the other hand, the government does not know for certain whether the price will fall below or whether it will be above that amount. It may not call for any sacrifice at all. But certainly the government are not in ia position to make a guarantee for the next five years, because they do not know whether they will be in power for the next five years; they might go out of power next year, in which event the farmers might be called upon to make the sacrifice for nothing.
But there is another reason why we are opposed to the farmers having to make that slacrifice. It is that we say that the farmers are being called upon to make a double sacrifice. For ten long years the farmers of the country produced at very low prices, and day by day, year by year, they were making considerable sacrifices. Therefore tod-ay the farmers should be guaranteed a fair price, a maximum price in order to compensate them for the losses they suffered in those ten years, without being -asked at the same time to make similar sacrifices in the future as well.
I believe the minister will recall that the policy at that time was bitterly criticized by farmers across the dominion. In 1946 the British wheat agreement was signed. Under that -agreement we agreed to sell Great Britain 600 million bushels over a period of four years. We were to deliver 160 million bushels in each of the first two years at $1.55 a bushel; 140 million bushels in the third year at a minimum price of $1.25 and 140 million bushels in the fourth year at a minimum price of $1 per bushel. In computing the price for the last two years consideration was to be given to the fact that wheat was sold at less than the world price in the first two years of the agreement. The Minister of Agriculture interpreted that -as meaning that we would have any losses in the first two years made up in the last.
Having that in mind it is hard to understand just how the $2 a bushel was figured out for the third crop year. The agreement stated that in setting the price for the third and fourth years the losses of the first two years would be taken into consideration. At the time the agreement was made for the third

Canadian Wheat Board Act
year the price in the world market was over $3 a bushel. Losses on the first year were 77 cents a bushel on 160 million bushels, which made a loss of $123 million. That works out at 88 cents a bushel on 140 million bushels. So that if you deduct the 88 cents from the $2 you have a balance of $1.12. This means that all we are getting for our wheat in the third year is $1.12.
The minister may argue that even yet that may be a good price. But everything indicates that $1.12 for the third year will be considerably below the world market price.
In February 1947 a bill to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act was placed before the house, and that amendment increased the initial payment to $1.35 a bushel. That was guaranteed until July 31, 1950. At this time the British wheat agreement was debated, and the government defended that agreement on the ground that it would prove beneficial to the farmers and that we were also under a moral obligation to allow Great Britain to have wheat at a reasonable price.
In view of the fact that it has been stated that the British wheat agreement was welcomed as being in the interests of the farmers of western Canada I should like to place on Hansard the stand this group took at that time. I quote from page 745 of Hansard for 1947, where I said:
In the early paTt of this agreement the farmer is making a considerable sacrifice. He is losing anywhere from fifty to seventy-five cents a bushel. In compensation for that loss, the government guarantees to take a minimum of fourteen bushels to the acre at $1.35 a bushel. The loss is being suffered on all wheat offered for sale, a loss of anywhere from fifty to seventy-five on every bushel offered for sale. Then surely the compensatory feature should also guarantee that that $1.35 a bushel would be paid on all wheat offered for sale. How can you balance a loss on total production against compensation on a part of production? It does not make sense or justice. Instead of $1.35 a bushel, w-e think the price should have been $1.55, which is the price at which we are selling to Britain.
And further on:
If in the next two or three years there is a wheat shortage, if crops are poor, the price of wheat will be maintained at probably a high level and will remain there. Then the guarantee becomes (absolutely useless. If that should be the situation over the next two or three years the farmers of this country, as a result of this agreement, are going to lose several hundred million dollars.
That seems to be the situation which has already developed. Then I went on to say:
I believe that the wheat agreement with Britain was fully justified, but it does entail in its early stages a considerable sacrifice on the
part of our farmers. We feel that the sacrifice should be borne by the people of Canada as a whole.
It will be noted that while this group supported the British wheat agreement, we supported it as a moral obligation and took the stand that the cost should be borne by the Canadian people as a whole, rather than by the farmers. On the other hand, if the farmers are to stand the cost they should be compensated by a long-term stabilization program under which they would be guaranteed a parity price for the future.
I know the government argues that there are compensations, and that the losses in the first two years of the agreement may very well be offset by gains in the latter part. The farmers are calling the government's bluff. If the government feel that the agreement is a good deal, then they should take it over. After all, it was the government that made the agreement. They did not consult the farmers before making it; therefore if there are any losses the government should stand them. We feel that the government should pay the farmers the difference between $1.55 and the average price received for No. 2 wheat and then credit that amount to the farmers in the five-year pool. If losses accrue as a result of the government's guarantee in the last part of the agreement, they could be charged against the credit in the five-year pool. The minister must agree that that would be absolutely fair and I believe that the majority of the people of Canada would support the government in such action.
It is well to remember that when we made our various contributions to Britain such as the billion dollar gift the industrial concerns in this country were not asked to accept prices below the regular price. The government paid them the current price and did not ask them to make similar sacrifices to those which the farmers are being asked to make under this agreement. In addition, the cost of subsidizing the home market during this whole period should be credited to the five-year pool; that is, the difference between $1.55 and the price at which wheat is being sold by the wheat board in the world market. While stressing this point, what we should really like to see done is for the government to bring down a longterm stabilization program under which the price of wheat will be guaranteed at parity in the future.
It is interesting to note what the government's policy has cost the farmers by compelling them to accept the price under the British agreement instead of the full market price they otherwise could have got. I have argued in my constituency that the losses in
Canadian Wheat Board Act

the first two years would be in the neighbourhood of $300 million, but apparently I was altogether too conservative, because the Searle Grain Company has set the loss at $296 million for the first seventeen months of the agreement, which has still seven months to go. They show, in addition, a loss to the farmers on wheat for domestic consumption of $152 million, making a total of $448 million which the farmers have lost as a result of the government's wheat policy in the first seventeen months of the agreement. Even if wheat prices should slump in the remaining years of the contract the farmers could never hope to make good those losses under the government guarantee.
I would ask this question:	Is there any
reason to expect that the price of wheat will slump heavily by the end of 1949? Mind you, for the farmers to make up their losses in the first two years of the agreement the world price would have to go far below $1 a bushel in the last year. But everything points to wheat remaining at a fairly high price for a number of years yet. I quote from the United States News World Report for February 13, 1948. on the back page of which I find this statement:
A price for wheat ranging between a 'ow of $1.20 and a high of $2 a bushel is being used by United States and other experts as reasonable over the next four years. Plans for dividing up the world's wheat are being discussed on this basis by thirty nations represented at the wheat conference now under way. Wheat still sells in the United States for around $2.60 a bushel.
That being the case, it does not look as though there was any great danger of there being a heavy slump before the end of the agreement.
If the government disputes the losses as computed, for instance, by the Searle Grain Company, I think it would be a good idea for the government to refer the bill to the committee on trade and commerce, before which representatives of the wheat board and the Searle Grain Company could be examined to ascertain exactly what the present situation is and what is likely to take place in the future.
Certain derogatory remarks have been made about Major Strange. I happen to know him. He used to farm just north of where I live, and I would say that he should have a very good understanding of grain farming. Incidentally while tie was farming in that area he won the world championship for wheat at the Chicago exhibition. He lived thirty to forty miles north of the town of Morrin where I live. The land is heavy gumbo which makes farm operating costs relatively high, but the yield is heavy and so the costs of production

are actually not as high as one might expect. Thirty miles east is the drought area, where operating costs are very low but yields very light, and so the cost of production there is higher than would be expected). In the district Major Strange used to farm the operating costs and the returns were average. He lived in that district for a number of years and from his experience there and his subsequent experience with the Searle Grain Company for a number of years he should have a firsthand knowledge of wheat farming and marketing. I want to make it clear however that I do not agree with his attitude on the grain exchange. On the other hand I believe that the figures presented by the Searle Grain Company have earned for themselves a reputation for accuracy.
Coming back to my contention that the government's wheat policy is neither one thing nor the other-it neither gives the farmer the world price nor guarantees the price for the future after 1949-we have this picture. During the nineteen thirties the farmers had to take a low world price. During the nineteen forties, from 1941 to 1946, the government asked the farmers to be satisfied with a lower price than they otherwise could have got. Those were the words of the present Minister of Agriculture, speaking in this house as reported at cage 806 of Hansard, and that still continued to be government policy during 1947 and 1948. So for ten years the farmers had to accept depressed prices; then for eight years, as the Minister of Agriculture stated, they accepted lower prices than they could have obtained; and the government has the nerve to call that stabilization policy, when for eighteen years the farmers had to accept either a low world price or a price lower than they could otherwise have received.
One might say that the government's policy has been one of subsidizing both British and Canadian consumers at the expense of Canadian producers. If the government are sincere, if they really believe in stabilization, let them bring down legislation this session to guarantee the farmers of this country a parity price as part of a long-term agricultural policy, or for at least the next ten years, and then we shall have this situation: ten years of depressed prices in the nineteen thirties, then ten years of prices below the world market, then ten years during the nineteen fifties of a parity price supported by a floor. I think a policy of that kind could well be called a stabilization policy, but by no stretch of the imagination can you call the government's present policy one of stabilization. If on the other hand the government are not prepared at this session to bring down a stabilization policy, then we

Canadian Wheat Board Act
should allow the farmers to have world market prices, and make the legislation retroactive so that they may get the benefit of world market prices within the British wheat agreement.
It is also well at this time to remember that there is no long-term program of stabilization over the prices of other farm products besides wheat, because the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act is merely a transition measure to govern prices during the period from war to peace. If anybody has any doubt about that let him look up the Canada Year Book for this year, which makes it very clear. However, Mr. Speaker, we in this group believe that a sound long-term agricultural policy is not merely in the interests of the Canadian farmer or the people of Canada, but is of vital importance in helping to promote world peace. World peace requires a well fed people; it requires stockpiles of food1, and stockpiles of food can be maintained only so long as optimum production is encouraged within the country and proper provision is made for carrying the surplus of one year over to another. History records that when that is not done, famine invariably ensues, which provides a breeding ground for pestilence and war. Unfortunately agricultural policies in the past have not encouraged a building of stockpiles of food. On the contrary they have invariably discouraged them by forcing prices down below the cost of production whenever reserves of food were built up.
I listened to the speech-perhaps I might also call it the bedtime story-of the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) last year. When he was discussing the grain exchange he chided a number of hon. members for referring to the exchange as-I forget the terms now-a gambling den, a den of iniquity and a few other things. I should like to say to him that these terms are very mild compared with some of the terms I heard farmers using during the thirties.

Whether or not these are the right terms to use about the exchange, he himself went on and proved beyond a shadow of doubt that the grain exchange is a gambling institution, because he told us one day he found himself with a thousand dollars which apparently he did not know what to do with. He went down to the grain exchange and they told him that if the sun shone he would make money, and if it rained he would lose it. No doubt, residing in sunny Alberta, he thought the best chance to take would be that the sun would shine. He put up his money; it rained over the week-end and he
lost his money. In other words, what did that mean? It merely meant that when it rained there would be an increase in production, and if we were to have an increase in production the price of grain would fall. That is all it meant. Therefore I say the grain exchange operates to discourage maximum production, because every time you increase production, every time you increase the reserves on hand, down goes the price and it is bound to discourage production.
I thought the analysis given by Henry Morgenthau was a very good one,. I quote from the Manitoba Co-operator of February 12, 1948, which reads as follows:
The most effective argument presented against the speculative system was a statement by Henry Morgenthau, Jr., secretary of the United States treasury under the Roosevelt administration. Mr. Morgenthau said: "Of all the economic dilemmas which periodically confront us, the farmer's dilemma is one of the most terrible and, at the same time, one of the toughest to solve. When the farmer does not grow enough to satisfy the demand, prices rise, he makes a good living-and millions of people do not have enough to eat. When he raises too much, the bottom falls out of the market, he cannot keep up the payments on his mortgage, and his crops wither in the fields. The problem of the agricultural surplus is a tragic irony in the very centre of our economic system."
Therein lies the kernel of the case against the system of speculative marketing.
In other words the situation is this: in order to benefit under the operation of the grain exchange the farmer has to pray for a poor crop. Then if that happens the price of wheat will go up and he could get a high price for the wheat he does not raise, which does not help him very much.
There has been a suggestion that the grain exchange should be closed. The government have told us that they are not in a position to close the grain exchange. I am not going to suggest that the government should close the grain exchange. All I am suggesting is that they should take the grain away from the grain exchange and let them play with something else. If they want to gamble, give them a set of dice and let them shoot crap. They could have just as much fun in that way, and I suggest to the hon. member for Oalgary West that he would have had far more fun and would have got a greater run for his money if he had used his thousand dollars in a crap game and not on whether the sun would shine or it would rain.

I hold in my hand an editorial from the Farm and Ranch Review which I think is a very good one on this question. I quote from the October, 1947 issue which says:
This whole defence dan be summarized in a single phrase from Mr. Jeffers' column- "through the ability of the trade to protect itself." Precisely.
The country elevator company favours the futures market because it enables the operator to protect himself against loss. The miller favours the futures market because it enables him to protect himself against loss. The same is true of the exporter, the shipper, the foreign importers and ultimate millers and bakers. In short, it protects everybody engaged in the wheat trade from loss, with but one minor and insignificant exception-the fellow who grows the stuff.
Thus it is no accident that royal commission reports quote with approval the opinions of all these people on the virtues of the futures market. All this reminds me of a fox hunt. The fox-hunters love it. The horses relish the hunt. The dogs have a wonderful time. But what does the fox think about it all?
That outlines very well the farmer's position in relation to the operation of the grain exchange. I believe some hon. members have advocated the two systems operating side by side, but it seems to me that that means if there is a guaranteed price all the wheat will go to the wheat board when the world price falls below the guaranteed price; and the wheat board will take the losses, and vice versa. When the price of wheat is above the guarantee, the wheat will go to the grain exchange.

The people of Canada would feel that if the government is going to take all losses then it should have a chance to make a profit as well on the wheat handled by the wheat board.
We in this group also believe in long-term international agreements. If you are to have long term international agreements you must have a wheat board that handles all the wheat; otherwise how can any government fill the international agreement if it did not have the surety of being able to get the wheat needed to fill that agreement?

The grain trade have used the British wheat agreement as a basis upon which to attack the principle of long term international agreements. They forget that the British wheat agreement was not a straight business deal, but was in part to help our allies, as was indicated at the time the minister brought down his early wheat legislation; therefore all the Canadian people should have stood the cost of the sacrifice and the farmers should not be expected to bear the burden. The grain trade criticized the long term agreements between countries on the grounds that whilst a certain price might be fair today it might be out of line tomorrow due to a rise or fall in the price level. That is true, and that is why we have argued that when prices are agreed upon they should be tied to the price level of the country with which the agreement is made. Then, if the price level rises the price of wheat will rise and vice versa if the price level falls. The result of that would be of course that our wheat would always bring back the same amount of imports. It would help to insulate the Canadian economy against fluctuation in world prices.
If we are going to have a stabilized agriculture and play our part in building up food reserves, it would be wise for the government to adopt a policy of government-approved farm storage. Then farmers building new granaries could build them according to government specifications, and in the event of future congestion in the elevators, these bins could qualify for the storage of government-purchased grain. I believe this was done in a number of states during the war.
We favour the wheat board handling of coarse grains. We do not think it is as important as the question of wheat, because generally speaking the price of coarse grains has reacted to the rise or fall in the price of wheat; but we feel that, whatever policy is worked out, it should be worked out jointly with the provinces. Therefore I was glad to hear the minister say that an agreement would be drawn np between the provinces dealing with the question of coarse grains.
In closing may I say that we hear a great deal about the prosperity of the Canadian farmer today, but in order to get the true picture one must consider the number of years that many men have been labouring to build up their farmsteads, and then note how many farms are in a run-down state and how many of the older farmers today are having to apply for old age pension after farming for thirty or forty years. Keeping that in mind, one can hardly say that agriculture today is in a state of prosperity. A stabilized

Canadian Wheat Board Act
agriculture may not help the aged, but at least we should bring down a policy that will help to guarantee that the young veterans and other young people who have started farming today will not have to go through the same degree of grief and hardship that so many farmers went through in the nineteen-thirties.

I wish first of all to direct some remarks to the amendment offered by the member for Souris (Mr. Ross). I take the strongest objection to the bad principle and bad practice involved in the government's action in presenting a resolution of this kind to the house to provide for a single bill which is really three or four bills. This was done last year in what was commonly known as the fifty-seven varieties or the Heinz bill, and apparently the government will try to do the same thing this year.
As the member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley) said, the only reason the government would oppose the amendment we have proposed would be that it wants us to swallow something we do not like in order to get something we do like. I would certainly ask the government to accept the amendment and separate these three or four bills.
As a matter of fact, this resolution reminds me a little of an excursion I take now and then into cookery. I am fond of scrambled eggs, and frequently I break three or four in a dish and scramble them. If you put one good egg in, one indifferent and one bad, the scramble is all bad. That is what you have here. You have a scramble and it is bad. We should get it unscrambled as quickly as possible.
The various principles or separate things involved in the bill are, first, the matter of providing pensions for employees of the wheat board; second, increasing the initial wheat price, in other words paying the farmer more of his own money; and, third, giving the control of the marketing of oats and barley to the wheat board.
I thought that this matter of control of the interprovincial movement of wheat products was tied up with that, but, from what the minister says referring to the marketing of flour, I take it that probably there is a fourth principle which should be separated out.
I cannot speak of this resolution as a whole, neither can anyone else, so I shall have to follow the example set by the minister and other speakers and deal separately with the things which it includes. The first of these is the provision of a pension plan for wheat board employees.
Not only am I unopposed to a provision for a pension plan in any organization, but I am strongly in favour of it. The provision of a pension plan by any type of organization is a great means of helping people to provide for their own old age, and we should all work towards that end. However, as far as this particular pension plan is concerned, I can really give no opinion on it until I see the bill and see what it provides for.
One thing I would say is this. In the agriculture committee last year, when the operations of the wheat board were being reviewed, there was a refusal to give to the members of that committee the salaries paid to the wheat board officials. I think we should certainly have that, and we should know what proportion of those salaries in the different brackets will be contributed to this pension fund before we give approval to it. That is one thing I would ask the minister to provide when the bill comes up for detailed discussion.
I would think the chief thing at issue in this provision of pensions, in addition to that, would be information as to whether the pension scheme is going to be one entirely separate and run by the wheat board itself only, together with the extent to which, as a result, it will be financed by the farmer's own money or whether it will be one that will be tied in to the general civil service superannuation scheme.
The second part of the resolution is to make provision for the increase of the fixed minimum price of wheat deliveries. This seems to me to be only a belated move on the part of ' the government to give the farmers a little more of their own money, money which the board should not have been holding back from them for the past two years.
This party, including myself, advocated last year that we should have a yearly pool participation with payment of pool receipts as soon as possible in place of the five-year pool now operating. That, I believe, was the proper position to take. It is what should have been done. There is no question whatever that any move to increase payments of their own money to the farmers has the support of every member of this house. I do not think anyone is going to argue for a minute that the farmer should not get a larger share of his own money that has been received for his wheat, and so far as that part of the resolution works towards that end, naturally everyone is going to approve of it. From the way in which it has been presented, however, this increase in the initial payment, from the way it has been put over by government releases in the newspapers and so forth, would appear
Canadian Wheat Board Act

'to be something in the nature of a gift to the farmers by the government, and I object to that. The general picture presented is that a benevolent government will increase the amount which the farmer will get for his wheat when he delivers it next fall. That picture is absolutely false, absolutely wrong.
Personally I would like to see as much as possible done to dispel any ideas along that line, that the government by this measure is handing out more money to farmers, to the wheat producers particularly. What is happening is this. The government is going to pay a higher price for next year's crop out of a great reserve of the farmers' money which it now holds. Why is the mistake of the past three years, of not paying out more of this, not admitted and the farmer given the money owing to him now, and given it in an open manner instead of in a semi-concealed manner?
This was what happened. At the end of the war the government gambled on wheat going down. The very fact that the figures in the British wheat agreement provide for a price drop to a dollar a bushel indicates that clearly. The government thought the price would go down. They gambled on that, but the gamble was wrong. The price went up instead. As a result of that, the board has what was previously an unknown number of millions of dollars of the wheat producers' money. This afternoon the minister indicated that amount was between $230 million and $240 million, I think. That figure has now been made public; and participation cheques should be issued on it instead of, as I said, concealing payment of some of this money only by the form of this resolution.
The third part of the resolution reads as follows:
... to extend the control of interprovdncial movements of wheat products and to empower the governor in council to extend the present system to oats and barley.
The control of the marketing of feed grains and also of wheat products used both for human consumption and for stock feeding, I take it from what the minister said this afternoon, is to be under the wheat board. Personally I would not object to the board having power to market coarse grains as long as they did not have the exclusive power to do so. However, the difficulty is that the wheat board has that exclusive power in the marketing of wheat. I take it from, this resolution and from what the minister said that if they put this into operation the intention is to give the board exclusive power to market oats and barley. As a matter of fact I took down one sentence the minister used

this afternoon. He said, "Price must be a matter for the government to decide". If oats and barley come under the wheat board for compulsory marketing, there is no doubt that is the case.
