Or even if he will re-read his speech I think he wifi find it. However, as I say, there is no question that if oats and barley are put under the wheat board, the government will set the price. I for one- and I know a large number of farmers who feel the same way-do not want to have the government set the price I am to get for oats and barley. There 'have been difficulties enough and there has been argument enough, I think, over the prices which have been set for wheat without getting the thing hopelessly complicated over oats and barley.
This afternoon the minister outlined something of the history of the wheat board. I should like to supplement this history by a few other details. The wheat board was set up in 1935 to market such wheat as the farmers wished to place in its hands. In other words, it was on a voluntary basis; there was no compulsion. Also a farmers' advisory board was provided for. As I remember it, this farmers' advisory board consisted of seven members, four of whom must be wheat producers. The act provided that that advisory board must be called together at least once a month. Furthermore, the advisory board had to be consulted on all matters of policy. That was done. However, when the Liberal government came to power in 1935 they disbanded this advisory board and put policy in the hands of a cabinet committee. As a result the farmers lost completely any control they may have had over the fixing of the price of their product, the marketing of it, and so forth. I must say that the government saw the error of this, and some time during the war reinstituted the advisory board. I do not think there has ever been any question,

Canadian Wheat Board Act
however, that the farmers have had really no control over the price of their wheat and the marketing of it.
It might be of interest at this point to read a piece from the Winnipeg Free Press of February 9. It says:
The wheat board is not and never has been a producers' board. It is a branch of the federal Department of Trade and Commerce. Under the wheat board act, it operates under the instructions of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, Right Hon. C. D. Howe. It is not responsible in any way to the western wheat growers or to any farmers. For all practical purposes the producers have nothing to do with it-except to obey its orders under penalty of fine or imprisonment.
That is the situation this board has come to under the present government. As I say, I for one do not want to see the grower or producer of oats and barley placed in the position of being completely at the mercy of the government with regard to price and so forth, through the power they can exercise through this board.
To carry on a little more with this history, when the operations of the wheat board started, the initial price to be paid to the grower was fixed by the board with the advice of this advisory body. The cabinet of course had to approve that. Later, of course, the thing was just set by this committee of the cabinet. In 1939 this practice was changed and the initial price was put in the act. At that time it was seventy cents. In 1943 that price was raised to ninety cents, was later raised to $1.25 and last year was raised to $1.35. From the remarks the minister made I take it that the government is now going to recognize the fact that it is better not to put in the act a fixed price. I think he said that they are now going to operate by putting in a provision giving the government power to increase payments from time to time. In earlier years no farmer was compelled to sell through the board.
To continue with this little history, when the war came on, the board, as the minister himself said a few minutes ago, took a monopoly position with regard to the marketing of wheat and all farmers were required to deliver their wheat to the board as and when they were required to do so. That war policy was continued by the act passed last year. Personally I do not think it should be continued. I do not think the farmers should be compelled, if they do not want to do so, to deliver their grain to a particular place, and so forth, and in a particular quantity. I have always found it hard to understand the desire on the part of a lot of people to force other people to do certain things. I do not
think anybody should be forced to do anything unless it is necessary or essential to the general welfare of the state and the people of the state. It has been well demonstrated that to compel farmers to deliver wheat at a certain place at a certain price is something which is not necessary to the welfare of the state.
So much for that. If oats and barley are placed under the control of the wheat board the government will set the price at which they will be sold or bought. That price will be set at the discretion of the government and to some extent is bound to be influenced by political considerations. There is no question about that; you cannot get away from it. A government such as we have in this country, which I hope to some extent at least is affected by general political currents, is bound to set such prices on political grounds. That is a situation I think we should avoid. The minister recognizes the difficulties of placing oats and barley under the board; he enumerated a number of them. I am glad he recognizes those difficulties. Perhaps, as has been suggested, this measure has been introduced with the idea of not carrying it into effect. Well, if it is not going to be carried into effect why have it there? Let us not bother with it; let us not have it at all; let us not have it in our minds to worry about; let us cut it out altogether.
As the minister pointed out, the marketing of coarse grains is a totally different matter from the marketing of wheat. The major part of our wheat crop is sold abroad, whereas the major part of our coarse grains is sold in Canada. In marketing our wheat abroad the wheat board has the world price to guide it in relation to the price it pays in Canada. In other words it is a marketing agency which does what might be called state trading on the markets of the world; but in fixing its prices it has to be guided to a great extent by the prices paid on the world markets. Of course in normal times, at least, its purpose has been to get the highest possible price for our wheat, because that operated to the good of the people of Canada as a whole and particularly the good of the producers. Therefore I think the wheat board has always looked upon itself as a sort of agent of the producers. The marketing of coarse grains is something entirely different. Immediately it raises an important domestic problem. Naturally the growers want as much as they can get for their grain, while the buyers want to get it as cheaply as possible.
If the marketing of this grain, which I say is a domestic matter, is put into the hands of
Canadian Wheat Board Act

the wheat board, then the board, which means really the government, is going to be subjected to terrific political pressure, on the one hand to put the price up and on the other hand to keep the price down. That being so the board would have to try to fix a price which would please both sides. That is an impossibility. The actual position in the country is that there are far more buyers than sellers of coarse grains. The sellers are chiefly in western Canada. The buyers are principally in eastern Canada, with some in British Columbia. If the setting of these prices is in the hands of the government I think anyone can see what is going to happen. The people who want to buy the grain are going to put all the pressure possible on the government to have the price kept low; and since there are three or four times more votes to be secured by setting a low price than by setting a high price it is pretty easy for anyone to see where the western Canadian grain grower is going to be. He will be right squarely behind the eight ball. I point that out to the members of the C.C.F., who apparently are eager to bring coarse grains under the control of the wheat board.
The western portion of my constituency is largely a coarse grain growing area, and I do not think the farmers there want this change; in fact I am quite sure they do not. I noticed a report in the Winnipeg Free Press that the Alberta wheat pool is opposed to this measure. The hon. member for Swift Current said the Saskatchewan wheat pool supported it, but apparently, from the account I have, the Alberta wheat pool is opposed to it, together with other Alberta farm organizations.
The general effect of the board taking control of coarse grains will be to promote conflict between the western growers of grain on the one hand and the buyers in eastern Canada and British Columbia on the other. I do not think the wheat board itself would want to be in the position of trying to satisfy both, or having to arbitrate between them and I do not think a bill of this kind, which will create such a situation, should be adopted. In the past the buyer of coarse grains always thought he should get them more cheaply, while the seller always thought he should get more for his grain. They both blamed the Winnipeg grain exchange, the railway companies, the grain merchants and so on for their troubles; but you did not have the farmers in various parts of the country at each other's throats, as you will have under this bill. Formerly the price was set by the free play of the law of supply and

demand, the natural economic law, and while everyone grumbled no one really got very sore.
In conclusion it seems to me that to have the wheat board market coarse grains will change the entire purpose for which the board was set up. It was designed to be an organization for the benefit of the wheat producer, to market his products to the best possible advantage. This change, to have it handle oats and barley, will turn the board into a consumers' price fixing board, and we will find the board to a large extent in the position of holding down the price to the producer to the minimum under which he will grow grain at all. So I say let us keep the board as a producers' agency instead of making it a substitute for the wartime prices and trade board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE ON WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a question of great interest to eastern farmers, and I am going to discuss it from their point of view. When I say eastern farmers I mean the farmers of Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes.
I listened' with great interest to the speech of the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness), who expressed some views which I share, though I regret not being able to agree with everything he said. I listened carefully also to the hon. members of the C.C.F. and Social Credit groups who have spoken this afternoon. Their speeches were most interesting because they revealed the opinions of a certain group of farmers in the west who would favour this measure inasmuch as they would be able to obtain a refund to cover the difference between the world price of wheat and the price they have been paid. If I understand their position correctly, it is that they agree with this measure provided that the wheat growers of the west receive a certain form of compensation. I understand their point of view; it is their business to urge upon the government the acceptance of that plan.
But I come as a representative from eastern Canada. Very seldom does the house hear members from Quebec, Ontario or the maritime provinces speak about wheat. But wheat is a matter of great interest to us as well as to the farmers of British Columbia, because we may join hands across the prairies for mutual needs. When on occasions I express myself along lines which might not be considered strictly orthodox from the point of view of party, I do so because it is my duty. Indeed I am sure it is my duty in this House of Commons to speak on behalf of my fellow citizens in eastern Canada, not only those in my constituency, but all the farmers, all the

Canadian Wheat Board Act
merchants and all the users of grain in eastern Canada. Some of them admit that during the war some emergency measures had to be taken, but they urge that at the present time we must consider the matter from the point of view not only of the east but also of Canada at large. My hon. friends from the west, no matter to which party they belong, have specialized: in wheat. Therefore at times they are surprised when one who is not a farmer, and who comes from the east, expresses himself on behalf of constituents and of eastern Canada at large with respect to problems as technical as this one.
Speaking as a Liberal, I am for free enterprise and I am against controls. You know that, sir. I have repeated it often in the house. In this country the east and west shall meet; the statement that never the twain shall meet is untrue. We shall meet together for common assistance and help.
Mixed farming has existed in the west for a certain number of years; but in the east it is followed to a much greater extent, and eastern farmers are dependent upon the west for help in the raising of their stock. There are difficulties of transportation and other difficulties which come from the incompetence of man. Those difficulties should not exist. I have already pointed out what has happened because of the incompetence of the feeds controller in the wartime prices and trade board. I am not particularly interested, however, in any individual. I shall be just as lenient as my colleagues have been regarding that fellow, whom I do not know. subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA

speechtext: Mr. EDOUARD RINFRET (Outremont) moved the second reading of Bill No. 8, respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: Is the sponsor not speaking on the bill?

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. Telephone development in Canada dates from the year 1880, when the Bell Telephone Company was incorporated by act of parliament. Although at that time all patents and lines were owned by the Canadian Telephone Company it was dependent on the Bell company, to which it sold out in 1882. During the year 1883 the Bell company operated in Canada with 4,400 rental earning telephones, 44 exchanges and 40 agencies with 600 miles of long distance wire. It controlled development in all the provinces except British Columbia, where the greater part of the system has always been in the hands of the British Columbia Telephone Company Limited.
With the rapid growth of private companies in the maritime provinces, the lines of the Bell company were disposed of in 1888 to the
Bell Telephone Company

Maritime Telegraph and Telephone Company in Nova Scotia and to the New Brunswick Telephone Company in New Brunswick, a minority interest in these corporations being now held by the Bell company.
A development of a different kind is seen in the three prairie provinces, where well-organized systems were sold to the governments of Manitoba and Alberta in 1908, and to Saskatchewan in 1909.
The lines in Ontario and Quebec are still largely owned by the Bell company. They represent a potential market of some 8,000,000 population. The 1947 edition of the Canada Year Book shows that in 1945 there were 3,151 telephone systems in Canada. Included therein are the three large provincial systems in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, smaller governmental systems in Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick, together with the system operated by the Dominion Department of Public Works, the National Parks of Canada, Department of Mines and Resources. They also include 24 municipal systems, the largest operated by the cities of Edmonton, Fort William and Port Arthur; 2,368 co-operative telephone companies, and some 527 stock companies. Of these systems 893 operate in the Ontario and Quebec area, in only 13 of which the Bell company has a controlling interest. Over 60 per cent of the total telephone investment in Canada belongs to the Bell company, and their telephones in Quebec and Ontario constitute 57 per cent of the total for Canada.
The Bell company was originally incorporated with an authorized capital of $500,000, which was increased from time to time. The company's present capital is $150,000,000 which was authorized and created by virtue of the provisions of chapter 93 of the 1929 statutes.

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: Has the hon. member the number of persons served by the Bell Telephone Company?

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
It has a potential market of eight million people. As of December 31, 1947, $126,420,900 of authorized capital had been issued and paid in full.
Mr. Ma'cNICOL: In what year?

speechtext:
the succeeding five years, that is, 1953 to 1957. Therefore the capital expenditures during the next decade will run into very substantial amounts.
It will be appreciated that it is a very difficult thing to estimate the construction program for a telephone industry for as much as ten years in advance. Such a program is necessarily predicated on views of industrial activity of business outlook for that period. One method of testing the company's views has been to look to the past experience of the company, particularly to the period following the first great war, with which the period we are now in has and will have factors in common, particularly in the field with which we are concerned-that is, plant expansion in industry and the development of new projects resulting from wartime research.
In 1920 the capital obligations of the company amounted to about $44,000,000. By the end of that decade of expansion the obligations amounted to about $160 million; it increased in excess of three and a half times. The company's capital stock increased in like proportion-that is from less than twenty-three millions to nearly seventy-seven million. The debt capital increased more than four times-that is, from less than seventeen million to slightly over seventy million. While *this measure is not put forward as being a true test of the company's requirements it is, however, indicative of the difficulty of envisioning the requirements during a period of expansion.
In 1920 the company's issued capital stock was $23,000,000. The company came to parliament, sought and obtained authority to more than treble the then existing issued capital of $23,000,000. That proved to be insufficient to carry the company through the full expansion period which ended in 1931 and the company again had to apply for a further increase in 1929. If in 1920 the company had sought an increase in capital of sufficient amount to carry it through this expansion period it would probably have been thought to be over-reaching.
Of course it is not intended that all of this vast amount of money which is required will be raised through the issue of capital stock. It is contemplated that something in the neighbourhood of half of it will be obtained through borrowings and other available resources of the company, such as depreciation credits, which will be used and invested in the plant to be constructed. As at December 31, 1947 the debt ratio was 33-24 per cent; with the last issue of bonds it has reached 41-6 per cent. Thus, according to the best forecasting and estimating, the company

thinks and expects that it will need the $350 million of additional capital authorized by this bill to carry the expansion and extension of its system.
The granting of the authority to increase the capital as prayed for does not leave it to the company to issue and dispose of the new capital as it sees fit. Subsection 2 of section 1 of the bill re-enacts the provision that was contained in chapter 93 of the statutes of 1929 and deprives the company of the power to make any issue, sale or other disposition of its capital stock without first obtaining the approval of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada of the amount, terms and conditions of such issue, sale or other disposition of such capital stock.
I respectfully submit that this subsection 2 fully and amply protects any and all public interests that might be involved.
By section 2 of chapter 41 of the statutes of 1902, parliament imposed upon the company the obligation of furnishing telephone service and telephones of the latest improved design to the public upon demand. It is therefore, I submit, in the public interest that the company be put in a position where it can fulfil this duty. To discharge this duty it is necessary that the company enlarge and extend its system and facilities to the point where it can meet the public need and furnish service on demand. As already mentioned, there are 94,000 waiting applications for service. By this bill, the Bell company is asking the authority to be permitted to go out, from time to time, after satisfying the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada of the propriety of doing so, to raise the necessary capital to enable it to discharge its duty to the public.
I cannot think of a better way to express the sentiment of the Bell company as to section 3 of the bill than to cite to you the exact words of its president at the last meeting of shareholders:
During the discussion of our bill, the banking and commerce committee of the senate adopted an amendment to the bill reducing the par value of our stock from $100 per share to $25 per share. In other words, it proposed to provide for the subdivision of our shares in the ratio of four for one. In the sixty-eight years of the company's history, our stock has not been split or subdivided. The amount paid into the treasury of the company by the shareholders averages $119 for each $100 par value share issued and outstanding. With this record there is a natural reluctance to disturb a condition which has stood the test of time. However, it was suggested by the committee that the division of shares would encourage the small investor to become a shareholder of the company,

Bell Telephone Company
and, to the extent that this action will increase the number of shareholders, it should assist the future equity financing of the company.

To finish the quotation:
In the light of these considerations, the company did not oppose the amendment.
It is immaterial to the company whether this amendment carries or not; it does not change the situation of the shareholders as to their proportionate holdings or as to their participation of profits. The net profits of the company available for dividends must necessarily be the same net profits regardless of the par value of the stock. The same profits will have to be distributed over a greater number of shares having the same aggregate value. I leave this matter in the hands of hon. members.
Section 4 of the bill is identical with section 39 of the Dominion Companies Act, with the exception of the substitution of the word "the" underlined in the second line for the word "a" to conform to the context.
Section 39 applies to every dominion company incorporated by letters patent and enables such companies to act and rely upon letters probate or letters of administration or other testamentary document granted by any court in Canada, Great Britain, Northern Ireland or any other of His Majesty's dominions, colonies or dependencies or in any foreign country when called upon to enter a transmission of its shares upon its registers in consequence of the death of a shareholder.
The Ontario Companies Act contains a like provision in section 62 applicable to all Ontario letters-patent companies.
Neither section 39 of the Dominion Companies Act nor section 62 of the Ontario Companies Act applies to the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.
Under the general law of Ontario courts will not recognize letters probate or letters of administration or other documents testamentary which have issued out of the courts of the other provinces of Canada or of foreign countries unless they have been re-sealed or otherwise authenticated by the surrogate courts in Ontario. The result is that if the company were to allow a transmission of its shares to be entered on its Toronto register relying upon letters probate or administration of any province or of any foreign country which have not been authenticated by the surrogate courts in Ontario it would have no protection and could not justify its position if the transmission became involved in litigation.
In the case of a deceased shareholder who dies domiciled other than in Ontario or Quebec the company is therefore in the position of either having to insist that the estate go to the expense of having the testamentary documents authenticated in Ontario or that the transmission be entered in Montreal where article 1220 of the Quebec civil code would
Bell Telephone Company

afford it the desired protection. This sometimes causes delay and some irritation on the part of the executors and their solicitors.
It is this situation which would be remedied by this proposed section, and its enactment would undoubtedly be helpful to those acting for the estates of shareholders who died domiciled elsewhere than in Ontario and Quebec.
Section 5 of the bill, which deals with wireless and radiotelephone services, is intended to clarify the company's powers under its original act of incorporation with regard to the use of the latest improvements in the art of telephony, including radio and wireless telephone and television, in providing the communication service which it furnishes. Wireless and radiotelephone is a comparatively new development in the art of communication and lies in the field in which the company operates. It is important not only to the company but to the public service which the company provides that there should be no question as to its powers to furnish service by this means. The company is already engaged in the furnishing of service to mobile stations in automobiles and trucks, which cannot be provided by any means other than radiotelephone. This can be extended to aircraft, railway trains and ships. The company is using radiotelephone facilities to connect its wire lines across the St. Lawrence river from Joliette to Sorel. It operates a radiotelephone service between Leamington and Pelee island where ice conditions frequently used to damage submarine cables and interrupt the service. It has furnished transatlantic telephone service by radio for a number of years in conjunction with the Canadian Marconi Company.
Wireless or radiotelephone systems can also be used to extend telephone service to localities which cannot be economically or physically served by wire lines, such as island communities-I have already referred to Pelee island-isolated communities in the northern parts of Ontario and Quebec and other inaccessible points, or where other means may be unreliable. The extending of telephone service in this manner will become of increasing importance as our country expands and develops.
Wireless telephone or radio is assuming increasing importance in the economical development of the telephone system. Developments in recent years have progressed rapidly and there is every likelihood that wireless telephone or radio systems capable of handling large numbers of communication channels over long distances may in many cases prove to be an economical alternative to

the use of wire lines. Since the economical development of the company's system involves the use of such new developments as become available, it is planned to use wireless telephone and radio systems as an alternative to wire lines where such use is indicated to be the proper procedure.
The radiotelephone is also very useful as stand-by equipment to substitute for wires in case of damage by storms.
Section 6 is intended to improve the French translation of the company's corporate name as it appears in the French version of the statutes. The French version of the company's act of incorporation passed) in 1880 and the French version of all subsequent amending acts give the company's name as "La Compagnie Canadienne de Telephone Bell" followed by the English name "The Bell Telephone Company of Canada" in brackets. The name "La Compagnie Canadienne de Telephone Bell" translates into English as "The Canadian Bell Telephone Company" or "The Bell Canadian Telephone Company" and not into "The Bell Telephone Company of Canada". The company has never used "La Compagnie Canadienne de Telephone Bell" in any of its publications in. the French language; it has always used "La Compagnie de Telephone Bell du Canada"; and the purpose of this proposed section is to regularize the use of the French version of the company's name which the company actually uses and which it prefers as the better translation. This proposed change has been submitted to the bureau for translations, which agrees that the name proposed is the better translation.
That is the bill that is before the house, Mr. Speaker. I therefore move that this bill be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, where members will have full opportunity to examine it completely.
I may say that it is the intention of the company to apply to the committee to have all the evidence submitted taken in shorthand, so that every hon. member will have a complete record before him when the bill comes back before the committee of the whole house.

speechtext:
My first words, Mr. Speaker, must be complimentary ones expressing praise for the way in which the hon. member who has just taken his seat delivered1 his speech. I want to compliment him on speaking the English language so well that one could not tell whether he was an English Canadian or a French Canadian. It is a great credit to him that he is able to speak both languages as well as he does. I would give a great deal if

Bell Telephone Company
I could stand up here tonight and speak in French. Although I can read French very well, I would not undertake to speak in the house in that language because I could not do it in anything like the way in which the hon. member spoke English.
If the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) were here I would not have to say a word tonight. He would1 be quite capable of talking until nine o'clock as he did on a former occasion when a similar bill was introduced in 1928, just twenty years ago. He has strong views with regard to this matter, but he found it necessary to return to Toronto yesterday on a matter of business, so I shall try to fill in for a little while anyway; and if I cannot fill in until nine o'clock there are several others who can do so.
The hon. member quoted some figures that I am not just sure about. Possibly they were the latest figures. But the latest figures I have been able to get are those from the 1946 Survey of Corporate Securities published by the Financial Post which I obtained from our own library here. I have forgotten just how many telephones the hon. member said are now in operation, but the latest report published is that for 1945; and this report says that there were in operation in 1945, 1,050,113, together with another 187,349-I presume that means country phones and subsidiaries. So evidently there has been considerable growth, for which the company deserves credit. We must give them credit for that.
Speaking of the Bell Telephone Company, I may say that on one of my last visits to Brantford I went out to where Alexander Graham Bell was born, a small farmhouse near the city of Brantford. I believe it is now a Bell telephone shrine. It is simply wonderful that a young Canadian boy out in the country produced and developed this marvellous organization we have today-because it is a marvellous organization and has done a great job.
There are, however, some things that I am not just satisfied with. Although it is giving a good service, and I am not complaining about it, I am sure that it could give much better service in some directions. Let me give you an example of what I mean. Last summer I was in the town of Mount Forest. It was a Saturday, and I had received a telegram about a member of the family having been seriously injured. I went to the telephone office in Mount Forest at five minutes after twelve and found a note on the door saying, "Office closed; go to the hotel." I went to the hotel on the main street in the town. The telephone booth was occupied by
a young man who was having an interesting conversation with somebody; it gave him a good deal of enjoyment. After standing there waiting on him for several minutes, I finally gained entrance to the telephone booth. I hope that the mover of this bill, in reporting to the telephone company, will suggest that they see to it that in all small towns where they have full and absolute control-a giant monopoly with no opposition whatever-they give full service to the people. I drove then from Mount Forest to a place called Mitchell, in the direction I had to go to see the person who had) been injured. Again in Mitchell I went to the telephone office and found on the door a sign reading, "Closed for the afternoon. Go to the hotel office." Again I went to the hotel, and I could get no attention there either.
That is not service. Generally they do give mighty good service, but I felt at the very first opportunity I should place before the Commons and the public the suggestion that it is not good service for a great public service organization to close down like that on Saturday afternoon. I realize that the employees are entitled to an afternoon off, but there should be other employees to take their places. The company should employ more help if that is necessary. The public demands service, and in my opinion that is not full service. I found the same thing in the far north, though according to what the hon. member said they are now going to rectify the situation in respect to radiotelephone service. The people in the Mackenzie river valley, at Yellowknife and all those areas up there should have received better service all these late years from this monopoly that has full control, that can do what it likes, that can give whatever sort of service it likes, which is not compelled to go out and seek business or to fight against other corporations for business. To my mind there is no excuse for not having given better servio* in those particulars.
I am taking this opportunity to speak in the hope that this discussion will attract the attention of the people so that when this bill comes back to the house a dozen members may want to take part in the debate; and it is a good debate in which to take part. Over in England I found that in every important part of the larger cities they had telephone booths on the street comers where one could telephone without having to go to a hotel or to a telephone office which might be closed in the afternoon. I think the time has come when this great company, which has almost a perfect monopoly in the two great provinces
Bell Telephone Company

of Ontario and Quebec, where most of its business is, should give a better service to the country and to the public.
The last time this company was permitted to increase its capital stock to $150,000,000, and now they are asking for another increase of $350,000,000. Today the par value is $100, but the hon. member said something about an amendment which would permit it to be split, four shares for one. That is a mighty big melon, one of the biggest ever split in this country. Imagine splitting $500,000,000 into stock which is now going to be reduced from $100 to $25 and sold. The hon. gentleman did not mention one thing stated in this report, that 21-7 per cent of the entire outstanding stock of the company belongs to the American Telephone and Telegraph Company.

the Bell Telephone Company had been bought out in the three prairie provinces. When I heard that I agreed with it. Whether Ontario and Quebec could afford to buy the resources of the company in those two provinces, I do not know. If not, I hope the time is not too far distant when they may do so. I am not a socialist. I am opposed to socialism. Where you have a great national utility, such as the Canadian National Railways, there is a strong argument in favour of the feeling that all these great public services should belong to the people. Mr. Speaker, I tell you honestly that I prefer to argue the case of the farmer to that of the Canadian wheat board. There have been many complaints to the effect that that institution is not working properly, and yet we are to give it more power. We know that many farmers manufacture their own feeds for use on their farms, and it is also known that any farmer, merchant or manufacturer of feeds will tell you that the handling of feed grains by the Canadian wheat board and the wartime prices and trade board has been most unsatisfactory.
Since the Winnipeg grain exchajige has been reorganized it is important to remember that any user of grain can now purchase any quantity of oats or barley, either bagged or in bulk, at prices which definitely give the user a larger margin of profit than was obtainable before ceiling prices on coarse grains were removed. If the farmer is of opinion that the margin of profit derived is sufficient he can hedge his purchase of grain, which guarantees him his profit until such time as his livestock is marketed. If the grain user is in the market for oats or barley for later delivery he can purchase his requirements at any time the price is suitable to him, or as already mentioned he can hedge his purchasing to establish his flat profit. The farmer is unable to hedge his purchases of feed grain as soon as feed comes under the Canadian wheat board. This is a composite picture of

the remarks that I have heard in my part of the country, and some of my western friends wrould be surprised to realize that these remarks are not parochial but apply as well to all the farmers engaged in mixed farming throughout the country from coast to coast.

I will give you the impression of many farmers that I have met from my constituency and from outside of my constituency. The farmers were taken advantage of at the time that the controls existed. My hon. friends will realize that I had something in my mind when I mentioned the Canadian wheat board; but the millers were responsible for it. Let me explain my case, and when I am through my hon. friends will be in a position to give their judgment, but in the meantime I ask them to be good to me and to be just as kind as they naturally are when I am not wicked with them, and I try never to be.
On such a bag of flour the government, ultimately the taxpayer, had to pay a subsidy of two to three dollars. I estimate that the loss to the treasury on these transactions during the years 1943 to 1946 averaged roughly $10,000,000 to $15,000,000 a year, a complete loss. Since October 1947 the government subsidy on wheat for the manufacture of bread has been removed, but at the time of the controls it was precisely the subsidy that accompanied the control that was the incentive to the miller to exploit the farmer and everybody who was producing cattle or hogs or even poultry. Notwithstanding this removal, there is still so much flour in the country that the general stores and feed dealers are trying their utmost to dispose of their surplus stocks at $1 a bag less than the present mill price. The surplus of flour is still so great that even the inducement of $1 a bag less than its value has not enabled country merchants to reduce their stocks.
The flour administrator, who at the same time is the president of the Lake of the Woods Milling Company, works hand in hand with the Canadian wheat board, definitely to the advantage of his own invested interests. The
Canadian Wheat Board Act

Canadian wheat board lack an appreciation of the need of close co-operation with the eastern farmers and the dealers, and they have established an office in Toronto but none in Montreal, the metropolis of Canada. They do not pay much attention to the demands of the Quebec farmers. No careful and sound businessman would consider raising cattle or hogs under present conditions. What measure of protection can he look forward to, knowing that the government- at any moment may enter into the picture and upset the price structure on grain to such an extent that investments would be severely jeopardized1 and most probably wiped out? I know that Mr. Lamont sent a telegram to Mr. King on February 16, and I understand that point of view. He is the president of the Northwest Line Elevators Association. He said, if the embargo is lifted on coarse grains we will make more money. This is a feeling that I understand, but there is something else. In business there is the law of profit and loss. Anyone who is engaged' in any business may make money at a time and he may lose some, but when he ends the year with a sufficient surplus it is considered a reasonable year, a good year or a very good year.
In these matters I have no objection to the farmers of the west receiving the world price for their wheat, provided that they understand that it is essential to their brother farmers from the east or from British Columbia to have the opportunity to buy and to obtain delivery of the coarse grain that is necessary for the economy of this country; and the farmers of the west who are grain growers growing- wheat, barley or rye or all these grains may make more money with one kind of grain, with wheat, of which we have a

surplus. We have a surplus of wheat, and the surplus, the overproduction, should be exported. It should be sold oni the world markets at world prices. I know the western farmers are good enough sports to suffer their loss when the loss is due to the world prices, and they are entitled to their profit. But when it comes to another commodity which is not grown in such quantities and just enough for domestic purposes, the story is different, because we Canadians must look after ourselves. I mean that the farmers of this country must help themselves before thinking of exporting outside of Canada any commodity which their brother farmers need here.
That is why I object to the control of coarse grains. I object to it because the Canadian. wheat board will not be in a position to do any better job for the distribution of coarse grains than was the old Marketing Act which was passed in 1944 or 1945. That legislation was wrong. It was a parochial kind of legislation, legislation designed to erect a Chinese wall around each province of Canada. It was nonsensical and it did not work. No one in the west, no one in the east, no one in British Columbia needed that legislation which was imposed on the Canadian people by a government that was not familiar with their needs.
I am not speaking as a lawyer. I am just voicing the representations which have been made to me in my office, on the street, in my home by many people who are not opposed to the farmers of the west any more than they are opposed to the farmers of our own province or the farmers of Ontario. They have the same responsibility for they have the same needs.

Mr. C. C. MILLER (Portage la Prairie) r There are several angles, Mr. Speaker, to be considered in connection with the matter now before the house. The resolution that was introduced this afternoon seeks to authorize a>
bill dealing with several different matters which we believe should be introduced in several separate bills. For instance, the question of pensions is mentioned in the original resolution. There is no question that in this modern day and age pensions are a commonplace thing. It is considered by governments at all levels and by business that pensions are good business, and they are now an accepted practice in this country. But at the moment we do not know just what sort of pension scheme is proposed1, and naturally we will not know until the legislation comes before the house.
Speaking to the resolution this afternoon the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said, as I noted it, that the support for
Canadian Wheat Board Act

the pension fund would be by contributions, half by the employees and half by the board. That may be and probably is a sound principle with regard to ordinary corporations. But after all, the Canadian wheat board is to some extent a crown company-it could be called a crown company-and it is dealing with assets which are not its own but are those of the farmers of western Canada. If I understood correctly the import of the minister's remarks, they could1 only mean that the farmers of this country, out of the proceeds of the sale of their grain, will have to pay fifty per cent of the cost of pensions for the members of the wheat board, its officers and employees. That may be fair enough, and it may be sound enough, but the members of the board, its officers and many of its employees are earning at least respectable salaries. I think most of them are getting fairly well paid. Are we to believe that the government intends that the farmers of western Canada should assist in providing a fund to give these men pensions? If so, I shall have to have a great deal more information before I can bring myself to support any such pension scheme. I am not against a pension for these employees, but at the moment I am inclined to say that I w'ould be sternly against any pensions where any part of the fund out of which they are paid would come out of the proceeds of the sale of the farmers' grain. The only pension I know of that the western farmers themselves can ever get is the old age pension, when they are seventy years old-unless they pay for one through an insurance company. Members of the wheat board and its officers or employees are just as well able to provide pensions out of their own funds as are the farmers of western Canada to do so for them out of the proceeds of the sale of their grain. Unless the minister, in introducing the bill, or at least on second reading of the bill, can show some good reason why this system of establishing a pension fund should be followed1, as I said before I w'ould be forced- to oppose any such measure.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, I think it is only fair to say-and I think our attitude in this matter is the correct one-that it is not appropriate that provision for pensions should be combined with the other amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board Act. If a pension fund is to be established, it is of sufficient importance to be incorporated in a special bill, and that bill could be a more or less codified measure setting out the system of pensions, how it is to be regulated, and so on.
When the amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board Act were being considered at the last session of parliament, an effort was made by some hon. members, and I think perhaps

mainly from this party, to have the employees of the wheat board included in the civil service. At that time objection was taken by the then minister of trade and commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) and one of the grounds of his objection was that the employees of the board were to a large extent temporary or seasonal and it was not practical to have them under the operation of the civil service. If the objection to the inclusion of these employees in the civil service was valid then, I maintain that it is completely in order in respect to the suggestion that a pension fund should be set up for them by the board. How in the world can you pay pensions for seasonal employees? Of course that could be answered by saying it is a mere detail which can be worked out; but in any event the objection then raised is one that I would now take to the inclusion of these employees in the pension scheme. Certainly before I give any vote in favour of this pension scheme, from the knowledge we have of it now, I would say that unless full answers are given to many of the questions which the opposition have asked in the past for information and particulars with respect to employees of the Canadian wheat board, I do not see how we can intelligently discuss any proposed pension scheme.
I suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that when he is discussing this measure, perhaps when he closes the debate, he be prepared to give information with regard to the number of employees and the salaries paid to them, because it seems to me that is information we should have before we consider this pension scheme. In any event we should not at this time make our final judgment as to how we are going to vote on this particular question. I would prefer to see pensions provided for these people; it is only the manner or the means of providing them that I might object to. Therefore on that question I would reserve judgment and deal with the whole question on its merits when the further particulars are given to us, as they should be when the bill is introduced.
The resolution moved by the minister states in part;
... to empower the governor in council to extend the present system to oats or barley.
When the minister was speaking this afternoon he stated, as I noted it, that they were taking or seeking to take the power to include oats or barley under the Canadian wheat board but they were not going to adopt any system of including them under the operations of the act until they had a system that was proved constitutional and workable. If that is so, Mr. Speaker, may I ask why in

Canadian Wheat Board Act
(he world the resolution contains these words: "to empower the governor in council to extend the present system"? In other words legislation is to be sought to extend the present system, not some other system the government thinks may be devised which will be constitutional and workable.
In any event apparently we are to have an alternative, if the legislation goes through; it is to be oats or barley. I wonder if that wording in the alternative was deliberate, or whether it was an oversight or a misprint. Does it mean that if the proposed legislation passes the house some time one or other might be brought under the operation of the wheat board act, or does it mean "oats and/or barley"? I want to bring that to the attention of the minister, because as it reads now I should say it would be interpreted to mean only one or other could be dealt with. I wonder if that is deliberate and if there was some reason for doing that, or if it is an oversight, or if it was intended that both oats and barley might ultimately be brought under the act.
The legislation which is asked for now is a little stronger than the present act. Hon. members will recall, of course, that the act in question deals with grain, and the definition is wide enough to include all types of grain. But subsection 2 of section 7 of the act as it is at present provides:
Except as directed' by the governor in council the board shall not buy grain, other than wheat.
As I said, that is a little weaker than the proposed legislation, but it seems to me this particular clause is none too clear. It does not say whether the government intend to actually bring oats or barley under the wheat board act, or whether they are just thinking about it, or whether they are taking the power to oblige the Canadian federation of agriculture, or whether they are really sincere in their desire to incorporate these grains under the board. It may be that they are taking the power-and I gather this is very probably the situation, from what the minister said today-hoping that time, the great cure for everything, will show them in some way in which they can please those who want coarse grains brought under the operations of the act, as well as those who are opposed to it.
Personally I have always felt that the wheat board owed its existence purely and solely to the fact that it was supposed to help the farmers of western Canada get good prices for their grain. The idea was that because of certain conditions in the west this wheat board should be created for the sole purpose
of seeing that the farmers got the best possible price for their grain. Now it seems to me that as we have gone along from year to year, from amendment to amendment, from operation to operation, the wheat board is in danger of becoming an instrument not designed to get the best possible price for the farmers' products but to make certain they do not get the best price. Today the farmers of western Canada want to get the very best price they possibly can for their coarse grains. It is equally true that the feeders of eastern Canada want to get feed as cheaply as possible. This is an apparent conflict which I submit the government itself can resolve without sacrificing the interests of either the feeder of the east or the farmer of the west. It may be that some scheme will have to Be worked out under which prices for the products of the feeders of the east will be increased; but I maintain, and have always maintained, that it is not good for the economy, not only of the west but of the whole of Canada, to depress the price of anything the farmers of the west have to sell. As the Minister of Agriculture knows, and as is known by all who come from western Canada, the farmers of the west are responsible for the prosperity of the rest of Canada. What the farmer gets for his products, he spends, and when the farmers of the west have little money to spend the wheels of industry in the east revolve very slowly indeed.
Another thing that bothers me about the powers which are sought here is that it seems to me there has always been in the minds of the members of the government some uncertainty as to what they are going to do or what they can do in connection with this wheat board act. This session we have a tremendous right about face from the position taken when certain amendments were before the house last session. For instance the Minister of Agriculture, speaking to the amendment moved last session by the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden), said at page 858 of Hansard for February 27, 1947:
The amendment, as I understand it, is intended to make this act apply to oats and barley and other grains in exactly the same way as it is now made to apply to wheat. I am qu;te certain that neither the farm organizations nor the farmers generally would want the act to go quite that far, either those who agree with the government or those who disagree with the government . . . Oats and barley, on the other hand-although this is not so true of rye-are grains which are grown largely for the purpose of feeding them on the farms where they are grown or of selling them from one farmer to another, or from one feeder to another, within the area in which they are grown, which raises altogether different questions with regard to the marketing of the product.
Canadian Wheat Board Act

If it were the desire of the committee to pass a. provision- such ias the one suggested, that is if the committee decided that marketing of coarse grains could not be provided for by order in council, but that we must make this act apply in all ways to oats 'and barley, the same as it applies to wheat, you would be creating an undesirable situation.
I agree, of course, that the government is not definitely saying that oats or barley will be brought under the operations of the board or be made subject to the act. The answer of hon. members opposite may be that they have not yet come to that point. Nevertheless it must mean either that or that the government is fooling the people. Then on page 859 the Minister of Agriculture went on to deal with the same point and summed up in this way:
The whole position in relation to coarse grains is so different from that in relation to wheat that I do not think you can deal with it by an amendment such as the one suggested.
At page 864 the Minister of Agriculture was on his feet again, dealing with the same point, but iie went a little further and enlarged on the theory of ultra vires, that it was beyond the jurisdiction of this house to enact legislation along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Yorkton. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) was more pronounced in his legal view, although he maintained that he was only giving the house the opinion of his law officers. At pages 862, 865, 866 and 867 he made no bones at all about it by stating that in his opinion the matter was ultra vires of this parliament.

It may be that the government does not intend to bring in any legislation to implement the power it now seeks to have incorporated in the Canadian Wheat Board Act. It must be one or the other.
We can have very little quarrel with the provision for the increase in the fixed minimum price unless, indeed, it would be as to amount. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) has urged consistently that the fixed minimum price should be substantially increased. I think it is only right and just however that all hon. members should take strong, serious and insistent objection to the

suggestion made this afternoon by the Minister of Trade and) Commerce that the price would not be included in the bill we are about to consider. It seems difficult to realize that the time has again come when parliament is asked

this is just another instance of it- to pass basic legislation, with- the ministers, in their great and wonderful wisdom and judgment, empowered to do the rest. Then we are to go home and forget all about our troubles. It seems to me if we are interested in the welfare of the farmers we should insist upon knowing where those farmers are going to stand in respect of payments to be made to them. We should know what they are going to get. If we go back home at Easter or when the house prorogues and the farmers^ ask us what they are going to get, and we have to reply that we do not know, then surely they will- wonder, and perhaps quite rightly, what- in the world we were doing while sitting down here in the House of Commons where we are supposed1 to represent them.
It may be that the minute we get home, or possibly before we go home at Easter, if this legislation passes, the Minister of Trade and Commerce will make his announcement in, his own good time. That has happened before, not under the present minister particularly; but I can- well recall- the fight that was waged in this chamber by this party at a time when we tried to get higher payments for the farmers when we tried1 to have the 1945 participation certificates paid to the farmers, and I can recall that on that occasion the Minister of Agriculture told us that what we were asking was not feasible or possible. But within two months after we got home following prorogation the then minister of trade and commerce, who is now Minister of Fisheries, made a speech in which he said that as soon as the House of Commons could reassemble, legislation would be introduced which would permit the making of additional payments to the farmers. Yet we had fought here for weeks, not only co-operative and anxious to help the government to make payments to farmers, but urging the government, times without number, to do so.
It is likely that that will happen, again. I maintain we are entitled to have this information, and to continue to argue and fight for it until we get it. I suggest the Minister of Trade and Commerce should reconsider his attitude so far as fixed minimum prices are concerned, and should let us in on the secret. For the first term, anyway, let us know what the fixed minimum price will be.
At the moment the minister under the' existing act has some control over interpro-

vincial movements of wheat products. This measure purports to enlarge that control. Until the legislation comes in it will be difficult to make any comment upon it, and I believe the sensible thing to do would be to wait and see what the extension is to be before we enter into any discussion of it.
I must repeat that I do not like the lumping of so many things in one resolution. It is not fair or sensible, it seems to me, and it does not help the progress of the legislation through the house when we find provision for pensions tied in the same sentence with a provision for the payment of an increased minimum price to the farmers. There is no relationship between the two things. It is bad enough to have them tied in one resolution, let alone having them in one sentence in that resolution. There seems almost a sinister threat in this sentence that we must either vote for the pensions willy-nilly, regardless of the arguments, that we advance, or we shall be accused of opposing increased payments to the farmers-which the minister knows very well we cannot possibly do in the light of our previous action and our desire on this particular question.
Speaking this afternoon on the motion, the Minister of Trade and Commerce paraphrased the legal opinion of the law officers of the crown, as given in the house by the Minister of Justice, by saying that one that would work was not constitutional and one that was constitutional would not work. I think that is a good phrase. The only trouble is that it puts other hon. members in a bit of a quandary, because we are now faced with a resolution which may or may not be constitutional. According to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has quoted with approval the opinion of the Minister of Justice, "if it is constitutional it will not work, and if it will work it is not constitutional. He says they are going to wait around and try to find something which will work and also be constitutional. And if he does he has to climb the almost insurmountable barrier which the Minister of Justice has already thrown across his track.
If the Minister of Trade and Commerce is correct when he states that that which is constitutional would not work, then I submit that only fortifies the argument I have made to the effect that the proposed powers in the resolution are nothing more than a mirage thrown up to entice the support of those throughout western and eastern Canada who desire to have a certain measure of control in coarse grains, and to have coarse grains incorporated in the operations of the Canadian wheat board.
So far as that particular question is concerned, I repeat that I am not at this stage endeavouring to offer an argument either for or against the inclusion of oats or barley- or oats and barley, whichever you wish to have it-within the operation of the wheat board. If and when the government makes up its mind actually to come before us and say it i3 going to do that, then hon. members like myself will make up their minds, based upon the legislation introduced, as to just to what extent we should support the government in any such effort. But at the present time, in view of the arguments we have had not only at this session but at the last, and in view of the nebulous nature of the powers sought under this resolution, it seems to me that we are tilting at a windmill. It is a mere shibboleth and a sham and will never in practice and effect be part of the law of this country. I trust therefore that the Minister of Trade and Commerce will accept the amendment and announce that it is his intention in dealing with this legislation to pursue the method proposed by the hon. member for Souris.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to the amendment to the resolution may I say I have listened with considerable interest to the addresses that have been given on behalf of all three opposition groups in the house in support of the amendment.
The resolution itself calls for three important amendments to the wheat board act: first, to make provision for pensions for members, officers and employees of the wheat board; second, to make provision for the increase of the fixed minimum price on wheat deliveries, and third, to make provision empowering the governor in council to give authority to the wheat board to handle oats and/or barley-for the legislation provides for both or either being handled.
The opposition, through the amendment of the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross), propose that instead of having just one bill amending the wheat board act we should have three. Since I have been in the house I have heard suggestions that we should have a second amending bill to an act that was already on the statute book or to one that had been put on the statute book at the same session, but on every occasion on which such a suggestion has been made the legitimate criticism was made by the opposition that the government could not have given sufficient consideration in the first place to the amendments they intended to bring in or they would have all been incorporated in the one bill.
Canadian Wheat Board Act

I shall not argue at the moment whether the amendment is in order, because that is under consideration by the Chair; but I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), who said he does not think the amendment is in order. Until the Speaker has given his ruling upon that point we must assume that the amendment is before the house, and of course it may be the question before the house after his ruling is given. But I think members will agree it is hardly reasonable to expect that the ruling given will be one which permits discussion of the very same subject on three different occasions in the same session. That is what would happen if the amendment should be ruled in order; because immediately the first bill proposed by the opposition was brought into the house every section of the wheat board act would be open for discussion; when we had disposed of that bill and the second bill was brought in, again every section of the wheat board act would be open for discussion, and when we had disposed of both those bills and the third bill was brought in, every section of the wheat board act would be open for discussion a third time. I cannot understand members who are urging that this matter be dealt with expeditiously taking the position , that that is the procedure we should follow. In the first place, on the legislation to provide for additional payments, we should have at least as long a discussion as on this resolution. Furthermore, I think each of the three bills the amendment proposes would require to be preceded by a resolution, so that instead of having three discussions on the wheat board act this session we should have six. So far as getting payments out to the farmers is concerned there is no doubt what the effect of that procedure would be. Some members may say that that particular bill could be dealt with first and disposed of so that payments could be made, but I venture to say that to many members of the house, the third bill would be of just as great importance, that is, the bill to bring under wheat board control the marketing of oats and barley.
All three of the western legislatures are now in session. One of them at least is halfway through its session, and the other two are approaching the half-way mark. If there is to be legislation supplementary to any legislation passed by this house this session it would require to be passed, if it is to affect this year's crop, at the sessions now under way in the provinces. must get through two other important pieces of legislation if we are to continue to make effective the other marketing arrangements for farm products. I understand my friends in the extreme end talking about straw. They know a little about straw, of course. I understand my friends who sit in the far end feel more than kindly toward our Conservative friends in this end of the house than do those who sit in the centre on the other side. They are co-operating to a large extent in any case out in the province from which they come, and there is no reason why they should not cooperate to a certain extent in this house. That being the case they do find it very easy to join up with our friends here to split up this measure into six different debates during the session, which would hold it up until the middle of June at least.
Having said these things with regard to the procedure which is suggested, may I for a few moments deal with what 1 consider to be two of the most important proposals to amend the wheat board act. In the first place it is suggested that we be permitted to pay more money to the farmers. The bill now provides for an initial payment of SI.35 a bushel, basis No. 1 northern, Fort William. I quite agree that the hon. member for Souris was correct when he said that last year the opposition moved an amendment to the effect that we then provide to pay more; but at that time we suggested that we desired to have more knowledge as to what was going to happen under the wheat agreement and under the legislation as then proposed in bringing returns to farmers before setting the payment higher. And we did not say that without giving reasons for it. We gave reasons which were referred to this afternoon by the hon. member for Swift Current, without drawing the conclusions which many of us have drawn on previous occasions.
I asked him whether there had been any pooling of oats and barley since 1932, and I might have asked whether there had been any pooling of wheat since 1932. The only reason why there has been no pooling of oats or barley since 1932 is that the wheat pools prior to 1932 made the mistake of paying too high an initial payment and were not able to pay any participation. They reduced the initial payment on wheat four times in a row and still were not able to pay the initial payment of fifty cents a bushel. Having gone through that experience once, Mr. Speaker, we are a little concerned about setting initial payments which, under certain marketing conditions, are apt to lead to difficulty. Therefore we said that we preferred to maintain the initial payment of SI .35 until such time as we had more information on hand.
During the year something has happened. During the year there has been a great deal of propaganda put on. I am surprised to hear hon. members who represent agricultural constituencies, and who should know the views of their own people, talking in the manner in which they have talked. I can understand people being in favour of the grain exchange method of marketing. In the past I have sometimes argued in favour of it myself under certain circumstances. I can understand people saying that under certain circumstances a farmer may get more for his product for a period of time under that system than he can get under some other system. But when hon. members begin to join with an organization which puts out a propagandist to make the best job he can of any figures that he can
Canadian Wheat Board Act

obtain in order to convince farmers that marketing their grain, or having the government market it for them, if you like, in their own way is not the best system, then I think men who represent agricultural constituencies should be very careful in repeating the information which is given by those who take that point of view.
For example, in the United States they eat eighty per cent of their wheat and they market the other twenty per cent outside the United States. In order to market that twenty per cent outside the United States at present the government goes on the grain exchange and buys the grain. Not so very long ago Mr. Truman accused the grain exchange of running the price up on the government by speculation. The grain exchange came back with the accusation that in buying 40,000,000 bushels of grain on the Chicago and other markets in the United States the government had pushed up the price of grain. To whom had they put it up? Not to the people of foreign speaking countries; they had put it up to their own government. I am informed that eighty per cent of all the wheat that the United States government purchased at these prices to export outside the United States was given away. In other words the people of the United States themselves are paying the price through taxation and otherwise into the treasury of their country in order to purchase wheat to give it away.
Some people on this side of the line, Mr. Speaker, take the position that by doing that particular thing they have helped the farmers of the United States and established a world price.
Let us take a look at what has happened in the United States. The member for Proven-cher (Mr. Jutras) made a speech the other night which caused me to go and get the statistics as they apply in the United States. He was perfectly right in saying that the farmers in 1946-47 in the United States got an average price of $1.91 a bushel for their wheat, and that is the highest price they have had in any of the years that have been under discussion recently. I will ask for the privilege of putting on the record a table* which will indicate that in 1931-32 the price of wheat realized by the farmers in Canada, on an average, no matter what grade and no matter what they produced, was 38 cents a bushel, while in the United States it was 39, both under open markets. For the 1932 crop it was 35 cents in Canada and 38-2 in the United States; the 1933 crop, 49 cents in Canada and
