For those ten years the average price obtained in the United States by the farmers was 12 cents a bushel per year higher than the price obtained by the farmers in Canada, all those years being years down to the first year of the war.
Then coming into the war, the Canadian farmer for the 1940 crop received 57 cents a bushel and the American farmer 68'2; in 1941, it was 61 cents in Canada and 94-5 in the United States; in 1942, it was 77 in Canada and $1.09 in the United States.
Then we come to the period in which wheat was taken over by the wheat board and handled by the wheat board exclusively. For the 1943 crop the Canadian average price was $1.13 and the American 81.36. For the 1944 crop the Canadian farmers received $1.21 on an average and the American farmers $1.41. For the 1945 crop the Canadian farmers received an advance of $1.15 on an average and the American farmers an average price of $1.50, and for the 1946 crop the Canadian farmers received an advance of $1.14 and the American farmers an average price of $1.91.
With regard to those last two years that come under this agreement, in 1945, the Canadian farmers realized an advance of $1.15 a bushel at the rate of $1.35 basis No. 1 northern Fort William as provided for under the wheat board act, and this bill provides for paying more.
I can understand the member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Miller) suggesting that he would like to know just how much more, particularly when we are told, as we were this afternoon by the minister, that there is about $230,000,000 in the treasury no\y which belongs to the farmers. The government has never emphasized anything else. The government has never suggested that we are going to be kind and give the farmers something. The greatest claim the government has made is that we are going to obtain, for the farmers as much under this system as they could have got under any other, and we are going to try to give it to them, not by taking something out of somebody else's pocket and putting it into theirs. We are going to give it by marketing the wheat and marketing it to the

Canadian Wheat Board Act
people who will consume it, whether in Canada or outside, at a rate which is reasonable and which in the end will bring the farmers reasonable returns.
Let us look for a moment at this 81.15 a bushel which the farmer has received as an advance on his 1945 crop, on an average. We have said to the people-and this bill does not provide for any less-we have said over and over again, that- the amount paid this year will not be less than 20 cents a bushel. Well, if it is 20 cents a bushel only, the farmer will realize an advance of $1.35 a bushel, on an average, for all the wheat that he delivered during 1945, and the farmer in the United States received $1.50 a bushel. There is only 15 cents a bushel difference in that; and, with the $230,000,000 which is in the treasury now, and with the $2 a bushel for the 1948 crop, there is no doubt in the world that at least another 20 cents a bushel-I am not going to wait until election time to start to give this information out-not less than another 20 cents a bushel will be available to be paid out to farmers next year, not only for the year 1946 but for the. year 1945,-the year 1946, the year 1947, the year 1948 and the year 1949. In other words, that will be five cents a bushel more for every one of the five years than the American farmers got for their wheat, on an average, in the year 1945.
Of course the figures produced by the member for Provencher the other day are correct. The statement he made was absolutely based upon the Washington figures, and the Washington figures indicate that there will be more paid out for the 1945 crop in Canada than was paid to the American farmer for the American crop in the United States. Whatever that amount is, whether it stops at $1.75 a bushel or whether it goes up to $2 a bushel, every cent of it is one cent more, after you pass $1.50 a bushel, than was obtained by the farmers in the United States, and every cent of it that is paid will be one cent that can be charged against this great loss that we are supposed to have taken in 1946.
Let us look at the difference in 1946. The farmer has already had on his wheat for 1946 $1.14 a bushel on the average, no matter what grade or quality or where he lived, and we are paying out at least another 20 cents under this bill, which brings his advance to $1.34. And, as I said a moment ago, with what is ahead of us, and following the same course we followed last year of being careful with the moneys in the treasury, we can pay out another twenty cents next year on the basis of experience. This would bring the total to $1.54. But what would we have to do if we paid it out now? We would have to go to the bank and borrow 5849-110J
money and pay interest on, it, and the farmers of western Canada are not asking us at the present time to go to the bank and borrow money and charge the interest up to them and pay them another 20 cents over and above the possible 20 cents we may pay under this legislation. They are asking us to sell their wheat at the best returns we can get, to retain funds sufficient to carry on and make sure we shall be able to. carry this through to the final conclusion. Then they are asking us to amend the act so that as time goes on we shall be in a position to pay out any sums of money we may have to their credit.
What has that to do with the statement made by the member for Portage la Prairie a few moments ago? He says he wants to know, before he votes on this bill, exactly what we are going to pay out. Well, he is arguing directly against what he argued last year. Last year he was arguing against knowing exactly what we knew we should pay out when we said $1.35, and now he is saying that we ought to write into this bill another figure-let us say $1.60 or $1.70. We ought to write that into the bill instead of $1.35, and in the middle of the next season, after we have sold wheat under the $2 bargain we have made with Great Britain for some months, suppose we are able to pay another 20 cents on top of that. He says we should not have the authority in this bill, but that we should have a definite figure in the bill. Well, of course we should not have a definite figure in it. We should be in a position, Mr. Speaker, not only once a year but at any time throughout the year, if the operations up to date have given them sufficient cash with which to make payments to the farmers-whether it is in the summer, in the winter or any other time-to determine that they are in a position to make those payments.
I have lived in western Canada and the western United States most of my life and have gone through three difficult drought periods before this one. The year 1893 was the worst of the three; 1907 was bad; the thirties were worse than 1907. And if we were not now getting high prices the drought we are going through would be almost as bad as that of the thirties. But we are getting high prices. I have gone through those experiences in western Canada, and I know that we paid out a certain amount of prairie farm assistance two years ago; we paid out another amount a year ago; this year we are paying out more than we have paid out in any other year since 1939 -somewhere in the neighbourhood of $16.000,-000-to the farmers in the well-known drought area of western Canada. I have gone through enough droughts in the west to know that this
Canadian Wheat Board Act

year may not be the last drought year. Under the plan of five-year payments that was brought into effect in 1945 the farmer knows that if there is drought he will have more money coming to him at an increase of twenty cents in each year, no matter when that drought comes; particularly after two years of the period have gone, as they have now, he will have more money coming than he could have had under any other system. A system of that kind is the best system for our country in western Canada, however it is put into effect.
I now want to make the point that there is nothing which indicates that the farmers
have taken a loss as compared with farmers elsewhere in connection with the marketing of grain down to the present time. Everything would suggest that, instead of taking a loss, they are going to get more money than they have ever received under any other system in any five-year period. Having said that, may I come to the next claim that has been made.
In this debate, Mr. Speaker, on a number of occasions the claim has been made that the farmer should not be made to pay for feeding the people in Great Britain. We make heroes and great patriots of ourselves by standing up in this house and saying, "Oh yes, we are ready to feed Britain; we are prepared to give them all the food they want. But when you do that, let all the people of Canada pay for it."

speechtext: We all say, "hear, hear." What is happening under this measure? Everyone in this house knows that a considerable part is never going to be paid back.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE ON WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
A very considerable part of it will never be paid back. And- to the extent to which it is not paid back, in so far as it relates to wheat, the money which was

paid to the farmer for the wheat is a charge on all the people of Canada. That money goes to the farmer, and' I think it ought to go to him. As we go along with this plan of marketing and make the payments which are provided for in the bill as it is now before the house, we shall be in a position to show in due course that the farmer will have obtained more money, on an average annually, than ever before through his payments based upon $2 for next year, the $1.55 he has obtained from Britain in the three years that have gone by, and based upon the w-heat which has been sold outside of Britain at higher prices running up as high as $3.40 a bushel, and out of a negotiated price from Britain in 1949. Out of all these the farmer will have obtained more money for his wheat than he could have obtained under any other system. The reason why I repeat that over and over again, Mr. Speaker, is that we have tried every other system. We have applied it under conditions that were just as favourable as they have been in the last three or four years or as they are likely to be in the next two years, and under none of those systems have we been able to get an average running up toward $2 a bushel, basis No. 1 northern at Fort William. So I say that this system is bringing to the farmers higher returns, spread over a longer period, and in a manner which suits the area in which the wheat is grown better than any other system [DOT] could suit it. For that reason I think we should get on with the job. vote this measure through, get the money paid out to these people who had no crop last year and make it possible for them to get their crop in as soon as the snow goes away in the western part of Canada.
There is one other thing about which I wish to say a few words, and it is in connection with this matter of coarse grains. I said something -about the procedure in connection with it at the beginning. Hon. members know that the coarse grains, with the possible exception of some twenty per cent, are fed on the farms where they are grown. Part of the twenty per cent ds marketed somewhere else. In the years when we have a big crop, more *of it goes outside Canada than in the years when we have a poor crop. This is one of our poor-crop years. We have little if any coarse grains to go out. There -has been considerable criticism with regard to what has happened since October 21 last, but hon. members are not guessing so much now at wh-at is going to happen in connection with the grain that was delivered before October 21 last. Three of the line companies are

Canadian Wheat Board Act
already paying out in connection with that grain. The pools have already announced their intention of doing so. And they all understand that the government is prepared to give consideration to additional payments which may require to be made in connection with the marketing of these grains. In other words, the same principle is being applied to the handling of these grains as has been applied in connection with every change that has been made in the controls since the beginning of the putting on of controls. We did not ask the farmer who delivered grain between August 1, 1946 and March 17, 1947, to carry the load. Arrangements were made to have these differences in payment met, and they were met. The farmer had a right to expect that some adjustments would be made when these grains were delivered. That is being arranged; and I am quite certain that when the arrangements are completed we will hear no more about it than we heard about some of the other problems that were discussed and later forgotten.
Then there is another phase of the question which has to be considered; that is the matter of enabling legislation. This afternoon hon. members of the C.C.F. group declared we should have asked the provincial governments whether or not they would supplement our legislation. I might just as well say that after we had said, some months ago, that we would have to wait until the session opened before we could determine what legislation could be brought down, the provincial governments should have approached us and said they were prepared to pass enabling legislation. I have not said that, and I am not going to say it. These provincial houses are in session now, all three of them. Immediately we pass our legislation they can indicate their intentions, and can quite easily put those intentions into effect by passing enabling legislation, if they desire to do so, and clear away any doubts there may be in our minds or in their minds as to whether the legislation can operate successfully from their point of view.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE ON WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Will it not be necessary to have some consultation to determine just what should be the enabling legislation? Has this government been in consultation with the justice departments of the provincial governments to determine that matter?

speechtext:
I believe the question can be discussed to much better advantage when the legislation before us is passed and before them. Then my hon. friend will see that the legislation gives the government of Canada absolute authority, to the extent that
we possess authority, to deal with the question. There is nothing in which consultation could assist. The legislation proposed gives the government authority to deal with the question, and as soon as that authority is confirmed by law the provinces can put through legislation supplementing it and adding any authority they have to give in order that it may be carried out. I presume they may want to come and talk to us about it, but the legislation will be there and will speak for itself.

speechtext: I asked if that were decided some years ago, and you stated you did not think it was.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE ON WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
No, that is not what I stated. I am not a constitutional lawyer or any other kind of lawyer, but I said that in my opinion this government could not do this thing by itself. I still hold that point of view, as I think many others who have been discussing the matter have come to that point of view. There is one question still in doubt in the minds of those who are considering this matter. That is the question as to whether or not the operation could be successfully carried on unless you had legislation not only in the provinces where the grain originates but also in the provinces to which you are going to send the grain. There are people who contend that grain put on a car to be shipped internationally or interprovincially, as we ship our wheat, is still the property of the person shipping it, and it can be moved over our railways to wherever it is going. But another question develops when you unload it from the car and sell it to somebody in Ontario. It is no longer the property of anyone in western Canada. It is no longer the property of the pool. It has become the property of someone who is going to distribute feed grain in eastern Canada. So a constitutional question is involved there, and I doubt very much if the farmer of western Canada would: agree to have this government buy his grain under a ceiling price and ship it to eastern Canada, only to find that no one had provided controls there which required the grain to be sold under a ceiling price.
This matter is not so simple as some may think. If we are going to get this legislation in operation in time to deal with the crop now coming up, or even to deal with the next crop, we may have to rely upon many discussions which will' take place when we have the legislation before us. But there is no point in going to a government and starting to talk about the possibilities under the act when we have not on our own statute books the legislation that empowers us to carry on the opera-
